The Pinax Standard

The definition of the embeddable scripting language Pinax — Edition 0.37.1, October 2026

1 Scope§

(1) This document defines the embeddable scripting language Pinax: which Pinax programs are conforming, what a conforming program does when it runs, how a processor refuses a program that does not conform, and how a C program drives a processor.

(2) This document defines:

  • the characters and tokens of a source (clause 6), types and values (7), declarations (8), procedures and the stack (9), control (10);
  • failures and faults (11), memory (12), modules (13), tasks (14);
  • the core procedures (15), the standard modules (16), the host modules (17), calling C functions (18);
  • the host interface (19) and the command pnx (20);
  • annexes: the whole grammar (A), the diagnostics (B), size limits (C), what is not in this edition (D).

(3) This document does not define:

  • how a processor translates and executes source. The shape of bytecode and the way it runs are the processor’s business, except for what can be observed through the host interface of clause 19;
  • figures of speed and memory use;
  • the features that are not in this edition (annex D). They survive only as names (reserved words) or are refused.

(4) This document is not written against one processor. Still, every example in it was run with the implementation in the same repository (pnx, libpinax), and the output printed is the output captured then. Where an example and the text disagree, the text wins.

Note

Pinax is a scripting language that runs inside one fixed block of memory. It has no garbage collector, no heap allocation, no pointers, no objects, no dynamic types and no exceptions. On the surface it is a typed Forth: procedures pass values over a stack, and inside a procedure values have names. The rest of this document spells that sentence out.

1.1 How to read this document§

(5) This document defines rules. Someone learning Pinax for the first time will find the manual easier to start with. This document is for checking a rule exactly where the manual points to it (“standard 9.3”).

(5a) The index at the end points, for each term, to the clause and page that define it. Annex B collects the diagnostic messages of the clauses in one place.

(6) Each clause has these parts in this order, leaving out the empty ones:

  • Syntax: how it is written in a source (EBNF, annex A).
  • Constraints: what is refused at load. Each constraint has a refused example and its message.
  • Semantics: what running does.
  • Faults and failures: when a run stops, and when a procedure fails.
  • Diagnostics: a table of the messages the processor gives when it refuses.
  • Examples: programs that were run, with their output. They show the rules; the text defines them.

(7) A change of the stack is written before → after, with the top on the right: a b → b a exchanges the top two values. “shall” is a rule for programs; “the processor refuses” is a rule for implementations. A paragraph number such as (3a) is a paragraph inserted later; a number once used is never changed.

2 Normative references§

(1) The following documents are part of this one. Where an edition is given, only that edition applies; otherwise the latest.

(2) ISO/IEC 9899:2024, Programming languages — C (C23). The host interface of clause 19 is written in C types and calling conventions. The header pinax.h itself also reads as C99.

(3) The Unicode Standard and its definition of UTF-8. Source is UTF-8 (6.1); character literals and escapes write Unicode code points (6.5).

(4) ISO/IEC 14977:1996, Extended BNF. The grammar follows its notation (6.2, annex A).

(5) RFC 4648 (Base16, Base64), RFC 3986 (percent-encoding of URIs), RFC 8259 (JSON), RFC 4180 (CSV). The standard modules of clause 16 read and write these formats; each of those clauses states how far it follows them.

3 Terms§

(1) In this document the following procedures are used in these senses only. A term defined in a later clause is set in bold where it is defined.

(2) processor: an implementation that reads, checks and runs source; the library and the command pnx that uses it.

(3) host: the C program that embeds a processor. It provides memory, registers procedures and calls procedures of scripts.

(4) state: one unit of execution of a processor. Everything is inside one block of memory the host gave it. Two states share nothing.

(5) source: Pinax text loaded at once, one file or one string. One source is one module (clause 13).

(6) load: reading a source, checking it and adding it to a state. When a load refuses, the state is as it was before.

(7) refusal: a load not accepting a source. The processor reports the place (line and column) and the reason. No code of a refused source runs.

(8) procedure: an action called by name. Core procedures, procedures of standard modules, procedures a script defines and procedures a host registers all look the same where they are called.

(8a) A procedure defined with def (9.1) has a signature and a body.

(9) signature: what a procedure takes from the stack, what it gives, and whether it can fail (9.2).

(10) stack: where values pass from procedure to procedure. Its depth and the type of each place are fixed at load.

(11) failure: a procedure whose signature has or fail reporting that it could not do its work. The caller must handle it at the next token (11.2).

(12) fault: something that ends the run on the spot (overflow, division by zero, an index out of range and so on). A script cannot catch it; the host receives it (11.3).

(13) region: where the bytes of strings made while running are placed. Each task has one; a mark rewinds it (12.2).

(14) view: a string value that points at bytes without copying them; type str (7.3).

(15) task: a flow of execution that takes turns with others inside one state; it changes only where it yields (clause 14).

(16) module: a named collection of procedures and values: standard modules, host modules, modules written in Pinax (clause 13).

(16a) Run (of a procedure): from when the host starts a procedure (pinax_run, the code of a load, a line of pinax_eval) until that procedure ends or stops with a fault. Stopping on the budget and going on again is the same run (19.5).

(16b) budget: the number of instructions one run may execute at a time. When it is used up the run stops and returns to the host, which goes on with it. 0 means no limit (19.2).

(17) In this document “shall” and “cannot” bind programs. A program that breaks them does not conform; the processor refuses it (what can be known at load) or stops with a fault (what can be known only while running). Each rule says which. “May” is a permission.

4 Conformance§

(1) A conforming program is a set of sources that keeps all the syntax rules and constraints of this document. A conforming program that stops with a fault while running is still conforming: a fault is part of what a program means (11.3).

(2) A conforming processor:

  1. accepts conforming programs and runs them as this document says;
  2. refuses at load a source that breaks a syntax rule or a constraint, runs none of its code, and leaves the state as it was before the load;
  3. reports the place of the breach as line and column; it may report only the first breach of a source;
  4. reports the kind of a fault (annex B) and the line where it happened;
  5. accepts the minimum sizes of annex C.

(2a) For every source, conforming or not, and for every bytecode container it accepts (pinax_load_bytecode), a conforming processor reads and writes no memory outside the state’s block and the memory the host gave it (strings passed in, bound globals, shared storage), and the run of a procedure with a budget other than 0 returns after a bounded number of instructions (19.5). A container that could do otherwise is refused at load (PINAX_ERR_FORMAT). Images (19.9), share files (19.7) and bound memory are data the host vouches for: the processor checks their shape, not every byte.

(3) The sentences of the diagnostics (the English messages in the tables of this document) are those of this implementation. Another processor may procedure them differently. What it refuses shall be the same, and the place it points at shall lie inside the offending token (this implementation points at the start of the token, or at the byte inside it where the error shows). Lines and columns count from 1; columns count bytes.

(4) A processor may add procedures, modules and host functions not in this document. What it adds shall not change the meaning of a conforming program, and shall not use the reserved words (6.6) or the names this document defines.

(5) What this document says it does not define (speed, the shape of instructions) is up to the processor. What it says differs between processors (default capacities, for example) the processor shall document.

Note

The line between refusing at load and faulting while running is the centre of the language. Types, the depth of the stack, names, whether a failure is handled and whether an owned value is handed over exactly once are all settled at load. Only what can be known while running — does a value overflow, is an index in range — becomes a fault.

5 Environment§

5.1 The state and memory§

(1) A processor runs only inside the one block of bytes the host gave it. After a state is opened, the processor asks the operating system for no memory. When the block is too small, the operation fails with PINAX_ERR_NO_ROOM; nothing is written outside the block.

(2) Every value of a state is in one of these places: a declared global (clause 8), a slot of the stack or of a local (clause 9), the region of a task (12.2), or memory the host gave and vouches for (bound and shared storage, 8.12, 8.13; strings passed in; KEEP_STR results, 19.3). There is no other place. A value refers to another value by number (the number of a row, a handle).

(3) A state uses no global or thread-local variables. Two states can therefore run at the same time on two threads. One state is used by one thread at a time.

5.2 Loading§

(4) A state takes any number of sources, one after the other. To load a source, the processor:

  1. splits the source into tokens (clause 6) and reads its syntax;
  2. reads it once from top to bottom, checking names, types, the depth of the stack, the handling of failures and the handing over of owned values;
  3. when all is kept, runs once, in the order written, the code written outside definitions.

(5) The code outside definitions (load code) can use the procedures and globals of its source. The code inside a procedure definition runs when the procedure is called.

05-load-order.pnx

use io .
"first: code outside definitions runs once, at load" io.println
def greet gives s str do "second: a word runs when it is called" end
greet io.println

Output

$ pnx 05-load-order.pnx
first: code outside definitions runs once, at load
second: a word runs when it is called

(6) When (4) 1 or 2 refuses, 3 does not happen. Not even load code written early in the source runs.

05-refused-runs-nothing.pnx

use io .
"this line is never printed" io.println
def broken n int gives r int do n "one" add end

Refused

$ pnx 05-refused-runs-nothing.pnx
05-refused-runs-nothing.pnx:3:41: this procedure takes two int values, or two of the same declared type

(7) When load code stops with a fault, the load fails, and the procedures and globals that source added are gone. Values that code stored into globals of sources loaded before, and what host procedures have already done, are not undone.

(8) There are two kinds of load. A code load accepts everything this document defines. A data
load accepts declarations and values only and refuses procedure definitions, calls and control (13.4). It is for text that is not trusted, such as settings files.

5.3 Running§

(9) The host finds a procedure by name and signature (clause 19), runs it with arguments and receives its results. A run has a budget of instructions. When it is used up the run remembers where it stopped and returns to the host; when the host continues it, it goes on from there. The budget does not change results.

(10) Below is a whole host program. It registers one procedure, loads a source and calls a procedure of the script.

05-embed.c

#include "pinax.h"
#include <stdio.h>

/* A host word: the script calls it as calc.tenfold. */
static pinax_err tenfold(pinax_call *call, void *user, const pinax_args *args) {
    (void)call; (void)user;
    if (args->i[0] > INT64_MAX / 10 || args->i[0] < INT64_MIN / 10)
        return PINAX_ERR_OVERFLOW;              /* as the script's own mul would: a fault */
    args->ri[0] = args->i[0] * 10;
    return PINAX_OK;
}

int main(void) {
    static unsigned char block[1 << 20];          /* the whole state lives in here */
    pinax_config config = {.struct_size = sizeof config, .budget = 100000};
    pinax_state *st;
    if (pinax_open((pinax_mem){block, sizeof block}, &config, &st) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;

    static const pinax_word_def words[] = {{"tenfold", "(n int gives r int)", tenfold, NULL, 0}};
    pinax_register(st, "calc", words, 1);

    static const char source[] =
        "use calc .\n"
        "def answer n int gives r int do n calc.tenfold 2 add end\n";
    pinax_str text = {(const unsigned char *)source, sizeof source - 1};
    if (pinax_load(st, "main", text, PINAX_LOAD_CODE) != PINAX_OK) {
        pinax_str why = pinax_error_text(st);
        fprintf(stderr, "%.*s\n", (int)why.len, (const char *)why.ptr);
        return 1;
    }

    pinax_word answer;
    pinax_find(st, "answer", "(n int gives r int)", 0, &answer);
    int64_t in = 4, out = 0;
    pinax_args args = {.i = &in, .ri = &out};
    pinax_err err = pinax_run(st, answer, &args);
    /* The budget bounds one slice, not the run: the host owns the stop (here 100 slices; a server
       would go back to its event loop between two). */
    for (int slices = 1; err == PINAX_SUSPENDED && slices < 100; ++slices)
        err = pinax_resume(st, &args);
    if (err != PINAX_OK) {
        fprintf(stderr, "the script did not finish: error %d\n", (int)err);
        return 1;
    }
    printf("answer(4) = %lld\n", (long long)out);
    pinax_close(st);
    return 0;
}

Output

$ ./05-embed
answer(4) = 42

(11) The command pnx is one host using this library. It loads a file, runs its load code and registers the standard host modules (clause 17). Most examples in this document are run with pnx (clause 20).

6 Lexical elements§

(1) This clause defines how a source is split into tokens. The syntax rules (from clause 7 on) read the sequence of tokens this clause produces.

6.1 Characters of a source§

Syntax
letter      = "A" | ... | "Z" | "a" | ... | "z" | "_" ;
digit       = "0" | ... | "9" ;
space       = ? SPACE, TAB, CR, LF ? ;
newline     = ? LF, or CR LF ? ;
shebang     = "#!" { ? any byte but CR and LF ? } newline ;   (* the first line only *)
source-text = [ shebang ] { space | remark | token } ;

(1) A source is a sequence of bytes written in UTF-8. Characters outside ASCII appear only inside remarks (6.3) and character, string and text literals (6.5).

(2) White space only separates tokens; it has no other meaning. A line break closes nothing. The exceptions are line remarks, the line rules of note and text, and strings, which must close on their line.

(3) When the first line of a file begins with #!, the line is ignored, so that a script file can be run directly on Unix-like systems.

Constraints

(4) Outside literals and remarks only the tokens of 6.6 and white space may appear. Any other character — ; { + and the like, and any character outside ASCII — is refused. Names cannot contain characters outside ASCII either.

06-semicolon.pnx

use io .
"done" io.println;

Refused

$ pnx 06-semicolon.pnx
06-semicolon.pnx:2:18: this character is not allowed outside literals and remarks

06-hangul-name.pnx

global 합계 int

Refused

$ pnx 06-hangul-name.pnx
06-hangul-name.pnx:1:8: this character is not allowed outside literals and remarks

6.2 Runs and names§

Syntax
run    = ( letter | digit ) { letter | digit } ;
NAME   = letter { letter | digit } ;             (* and not a reserved word *)
PATH   = NAME "." member { "." member } ;        (* no space around a dot *)
member = letter { letter | digit } ;              (* a reserved word too: json.array *)

(1) Letters, digits and underscores that follow each other are read whole, as one run, and only then classified. A run that is a reserved word (6.6) is a reserved word; one that begins with a digit is a number (6.4); anything else is a name. So remark is a name, not a remark, and 12ab is neither a name nor a number.

(2) A path is names joined by dots, with no space around a dot. Inside a run of text a dot appears only in paths and in numbers (2.5). A dot that no name, digit, dot or quote follows is a token of its own: it ends a statement (10.8), also when it is written against the run before it (7 sq.). A path names a procedure of a module (io.println), a field of a record (p.x) or a constant (str.digit).

(3) A run after a dot is part of the path even when it is a reserved word (json.array). The first run of a path cannot be a reserved word.

Constraints

(4) A dot inside a path shall be followed by a name, with no space.

06-dot-apart.pnx

use io .
"x" io. println

Refused

$ pnx 06-dot-apart.pnx
06-dot-apart.pnx:2:5: this name is not declared before this place

(5) Names are case-sensitive: Total and total are different names. A name is at most 31 bytes long (annex C).

6.3 Remarks§

Syntax
remark       = line-remark | block-remark ;
line-remark  = "rem" { ? any byte but CR and LF ? } newline ;   (* "rem" as a whole run *)
block-remark = "note" TAG { ? any byte but CR and LF ? } newline
               { ? a line that does not start with TAG at the first column ? newline }
               TAG ;                                             (* at the first column *)
TAG          = NAME ;

(1) The run rem makes a remark from there to the end of the line, but only when the whole run is rem: remark is a name. The end of the file stands in for the line break.

(2) The run note and a tag open a block remark. The remark is closed by a line that starts, in the first column, with that tag, not followed by a letter or digit. An indented tag, or a longer run that begins with the tag (DOCUMENT), does not close it.

06-remarks.pnx

use io .
rem A line remark runs to the end of its line.
"one" io.println rem a remark may follow code
note DOC
A block remark runs to a line that starts with its tag.
  DOC indented does not close it, nor does DOCUMENT.
DOC
global remark int        rem "remark" is a name: rem must stand alone
global notes int
3 set remark
"two" io.println

Output

$ pnx 06-remarks.pnx
one
two

(3) A tool may read the remark right before a declaration as its description. There is no separate mark for documentation remarks.

(4) Where a new name is due, the runs rem, note and text open neither a remark nor a text: they are procedures of the language there, and refused as names (9.5). A new name is due after a procedure that declares one (def, forward, extern, test, global, const, array, list, pool, queue, buffer, tasks, record, type, index), after to, set and as, and right after a comma of a signature or at the name place of to, or_else to, do to, ref and args. In the body of a record text is always refused; rem and note are remarks there, as everywhere else.

06-remark-name.pnx

global note int

Refused

$ pnx 06-remark-name.pnx
06-remark-name.pnx:1:8: note is a procedure of the language; choose another name

6.4 Numbers§

Syntax
sign        = "+" | "-" ;                    (* attached: no space before the digits *)
digits      = digit { [ "_" ] digit } ;
INT         = [ sign ] ( digits | "0x" hex-digits | "0b" bit-digits ) ;
DEC         = [ sign ] digits "." digits ;   (* a decimal, 7.5; no exponent *)
hex-digits  = hex { [ "_" ] hex } ;          (* hex: digit, A-F, a-f *)
bit-digits  = bit { [ "_" ] bit } ;          (* bit: 0, 1 *)

(1) The value of an integer literal is a 64-bit two’s complement integer (7.1). It is written in decimal, hexadecimal (0x) or binary (0b). There is no octal form: 0755 is decimal 755.

(2) A sign is part of a number when it is attached to the digits: -42 is one number. Addition and subtraction are the procedures add and sub; + and - are not characters of their own.

(3) One underscore may stand between two digits; it is not part of the value. 0x and 0b are lower case only; hexadecimal digits A–F may be either case.

06-numbers.pnx

use io .
use str .
1_000_000 str.to_str io.println     rem underscores between digits
0xFF str.to_str io.println          rem hexadecimal
0b1010 str.to_str io.println        rem binary
0755 str.to_str io.println          rem decimal: there is no octal form
-42 str.to_str io.println           rem the sign is part of the number
-9223372036854775808 str.to_str io.println
'A' str.to_str io.println           rem a character is a u8: one byte
U'가' str.to_str io.println          rem U'..' is one code point

Output

$ pnx 06-numbers.pnx
1000000
255
10
755
-42
-9223372036854775808
65
44032
Constraints

(4) A number directly followed by a letter, an underscore or a dot is refused.

06-number-letters.pnx

use io .
12ab drop

Refused

$ pnx 06-number-letters.pnx
06-number-letters.pnx:2:3: a number must not run into letters, an underscore or a dot

(5) A space between a sign and its digits is refused.

06-sign-apart.pnx

use io .
- 7 drop

Refused

$ pnx 06-sign-apart.pnx
06-sign-apart.pnx:2:1: a sign is attached to its number; arithmetic uses procedures (add, sub)

(6) A value outside the range of a 64-bit signed integer (−263 to 263−1) is refused.

06-int-range.pnx

9223372036854775808 drop

Refused

$ pnx 06-int-range.pnx
06-int-range.pnx:1:1: the integer does not fit in 64 bits

(7) An underscore stands only between two digits, one at a time: 1__000 _1 1_ 0x_F are refused.

06-underscore.pnx

1__000 drop

Refused

$ pnx 06-underscore.pnx
06-underscore.pnx:1:2: an underscore stands between two digits

(8) A number with a point and digits on both sides and no exponent is a decimal literal (12.50, 7.5). At most 18 digits follow the point, and the digits together, as an integer, shall fit in 64 bits. A number with an exponent (2e3, 2.5e0) or a hexadecimal one with p (0x1.8p1) is a float literal (7.7). It is rounded once to the nearest value, and a value too large is an infinity.

6.5 Characters, strings, text§

Syntax
CHAR      = [ "U" ] "'" ( char-byte | escape ) "'" ;
STRING    = '"' { string-byte | escape } '"' ;          (* closes on the same line *)
RAWSTRING = "r" '"' { raw-byte } '"' ;                  (* no escapes; same line *)
TEXT      = "text" TAG { blank } newline
            { ? a line that does not start with TAG at the first column ? newline }
            TAG ;                                       (* at the first column *)
escape    = "\\" | '\"' | "\'" | "\a" | "\b" | "\f" | "\n" | "\r" | "\t" | "\v" | "\0"
          | "\x" hex hex | "\u" hex hex hex hex | "\U" hex hex hex hex hex hex hex hex ;
BOOL      = "true" | "false" ;

(1) The value of a character literal is, without a prefix, the u8 of one byte, and with U the u32 of one code point (7.6; 'A' is the u8 65, U'가' the u32 44032).

(2) The value of a string literal is a str. The fourteen escapes above are the only ones, each of a fixed length. \u and \U put a Unicode code point (not a surrogate, at most U+10FFFF) as UTF-8; \x puts one byte.

(3) A raw string is the run r with " directly after it. Backslash is an ordinary character, and there is no way to put a " inside. It is for paths and regular expressions.

(4) A text literal writes several lines as they are. The text TAG line may hold only spaces after the tag; the value is the lines after it, up to the line of the closing tag. The line break right before the closing line is not part of the value. Escapes are not decoded. The type is str.

06-strings.pnx

use io .
"tab:\t| quote:\" | hex:\x41 | code point:\u00e9" io.println
r"C:\new\table" io.println          rem raw: backslashes stay
text END
  A text literal keeps its lines as written, "quotes" and \n too.
END
io.println

6.6 Reserved words and punctuation§

Syntax
punct    = "(" | ")" | "," | "." ;              (* a lone dot ends a statement, (2) *)
token    = reserved | NAME | PATH | INT | CHAR | STRING | RAWSTRING | TEXT | BOOL | punct ;
reserved = "rem" | "note" | "text" | "true" | "false" | "pinax"
         | "use" | "as" | "export"
         | "procedure" | "global" | "const" | "array" | "list" | "pool" | "queue" | "buffer"
         | "tasks" | "record" | "type" | "extern" | "from" | "forward" | "index" | "bound" | "shared"
         | "make" | "test" | "row" | "assign" | "big_endian" | "columns"
         | "gives" | "or" | "fail" | "owned"
         | "to" | "do" | "end" | "if" | "else" | "loop" | "while" | "until" | "break"
         | "case" | "of" | "otherwise" | "return" | "or_fail" | "or_return" | "or_else" | "cat"
         | "defer" | "set" | "fits" | "set_order" | "get_order"
         | "def" | "ref" | "match" | "when" | "continue" | "args" ;

(1) The list of reserved words is closed. A reserved word cannot be a name. The names of the old forms (word while until case of cat) stay reserved only so that they are refused: using one is refused with a message that names the new form (annex B).

(2) or is a reserved word only inside a signature (or fail). In the body of a procedure or is a core procedure (logical or).

(3) The only punctuation is ( ) , and the dot that ends a statement (6.2 (2)). Each is a token of its own even when written against other text: 7 sq. is three tokens.

(3a) Lists that a procedure reads when it is compiled (names, a signature, a size, the items of args) are not wrapped in parentheses; they follow the procedure: names (to a, set_order io str .), a signature (def sq n int gives int do … end), a size (str 32), items (args "id=" id . cat). A list ends with a period or with a procedure such as do or end. The values a procedure takes when it runs come before it (2 3 add). Parentheses are left only in the value lists of assign and row.

(4) The names of types (int str bool …) and of core procedures (add dup …) are not reserved words but names declared in advance. Declaring them again is refused by the rule against hiding names (9.5).

(5) make is reserved for a future feature and refused when used (annex D).

6.7 Format version§

Syntax
source = [ "pinax" INT ] { item } ;

(1) Writing pinax and an integer as the first tokens of a source states the format version the source follows. This document defines version 2. Without it, a source is read as version 2.

06-version.pnx

pinax 2
use io .
"written for format version 2" io.println

Output

$ pnx 06-version.pnx
written for format version 2
Constraints

(2) A source that states a version the processor does not read is refused.

06-version-other.pnx

use io .
"never read" io.println

Refused

$ pnx 06-version-other.pnx
06-version-other.pnx:1:7: this source is written for another format version; this build reads version 2

7 Types and values§

(1) Every value has a type fixed at load. Values do not carry their type while running, and no procedure asks for a type while running. A program whose types do not match is refused at load.

(2) The types are:

TypeValues
int64-bit two’s complement integers (7.1)
dec Ndecimals with N digits after the point, N from 0 to 18 (7.5)
floatIEEE 754 binary64 floating-point numbers (7.7)
u8 u16 u32 u64 i8 i16 i32unsigned and signed integers of that width (7.6); u8 is a byte, u32 a code point
booltrue, false (7.2)
stra view of bytes (7.3); only in locals, arguments and results
str Nstored text of up to N bytes (7.3); in globals, cells of arrays, fields of records
errthe error code of a failure (11.1)
declared typea type made with type NAME base: the same representation as its base, a different type (7.4)
rowone row of a table of records (array, list, pool); the type is named after the table (8.8)
handlea number that refers to an object the host gave; the host names the type (19.6)
blockthe type of a procedure value, named by type NAME proc signature end (10.5)
regexa regular expression program (16.7); visible only in a source that has use rex
buffera parameter type: it takes a buffer the script declared (8.7, 9.9, 19.3)

(3) Globals, cells of arrays and fields of records start at zero: int 0, bool false, str N the empty text, a row “none” (8.8).

7.1 Integers§

(1) The values of int are the integers from −263 to 263−1, the same on every processor.

(2) The arithmetic procedures add sub mul div mod neg abs stop with the fault overflow when the result is out of range (11.3). There are procedures that wrap (wrap_add …), that stop at the edge (sat_add …), and that report overflow as a failure (chk_add …) (15.1).

(3) div rounds toward zero, and the result of mod has the sign of the dividend (a b div b mul a b mod add is a). floor_div and floor_mod round down. Division by zero is the fault div_zero.

07-int.pnx

use io .
use str .
9223372036854775807 str.to_str io.println          rem the largest int
7 2 div str.to_str io.println                       rem division rounds toward zero
-7 2 div str.to_str io.println
-7 2 mod str.to_str io.println                      rem the remainder has the sign of the dividend
-7 2 floor_div str.to_str io.println                rem floor_div rounds down
9223372036854775807 1 wrap_add str.to_str io.println    rem wrap_add wraps around
9223372036854775807 1 sat_add str.to_str io.println     rem sat_add stops at the edge

Output

$ pnx 07-int.pnx
9223372036854775807
3
-3
-1
-4
-9223372036854775808
9223372036854775807
Faults

(4) An overflow ends the run on the spot. In the example below the code after the line that overflows does not run.

07-int-overflow.pnx

global big int
9223372036854775807 set big
"before" io.println
big 1 add set big
"never printed" io.println

$ pnx 07-int-overflow.pnx

07-int-overflow.pnx:5: integer overflow

7.2 Booleans§

(1) bool has two values, true and false. Comparison procedures (eq lt …) give them; if and the logical procedures (and or not) take them.

07-bool.pnx

use io .
use str .
3 4 lt if "3 is less than 4" else "no" end io.println
true false or not if "never" else "true false or not is false" end io.println

Output

$ pnx 07-bool.pnx
3 is less than 4
true false or not is false
Constraints

(2) bool and int do not convert into each other. An int cannot stand where a condition goes, nor a bool where arithmetic goes.

07-bool-not-int.pnx

1 if 2 drop end

Refused

$ pnx 07-bool-not-int.pnx
07-bool-not-int.pnx:1:3: a bool is expected here

07-int-not-bool.pnx

Refused

$ pnx 07-int-not-bool.pnx
07-int-not-bool.pnx:1:8: this procedure takes two int values, or two of the same declared type

7.3 Strings§

(1) A string is a sequence of bytes. There is no rule that it be UTF-8: procedures that work on bytes read bytes, and procedures that work on characters (str.char_count and so on) read UTF-8.

(2) There are two string types.

  • str is a view: the start and length of bytes that are somewhere (a literal, the text of a global, a buffer, the region). Making one copies no bytes. It lives only in locals, arguments, results and on the stack.
  • str N is stored text. It takes N bytes of room and copies the bytes put into it. It is used only in globals, cells of arrays and lists, and fields of records. Reading it gives a str view of that room.

07-str.pnx

use io .
use str .
global name str 8                 rem stored text: up to 8 bytes, copied in
def show s str do args "[" s "] " s str.len . cat io.println end
"Pinax" set name
name show
"hello, world" 7 str.skip show        rem a view: no byte is copied

Output

$ pnx 07-str.pnx
[Pinax] 5
[world] 5
Constraints

(3) str for a global, an array or a field of a record is refused: the bytes a view points at may disappear before that place does.

07-str-global.pnx

global name str

Refused

$ pnx 07-str-global.pnx
07-str-global.pnx:2:1: stored text is written str N, N the size in bytes; a str view lives only in locals, arguments and results
Faults

(4) Putting text longer than N bytes into a str N place with no guard after the store stops with the fault range. It is not cut.

07-str-too-long.pnx

use io .
global name str 4
"four" set name
"more than four" set name

Fault

$ pnx 07-str-too-long.pnx
07-str-too-long.pnx:4: index out of range

(4a) A store into a str N place (a field with to, a global or a cell with set) may be followed by a guard (11.2). Then a text longer than N bytes is the failure range, and the place keeps what it held; a shorter text is stored and the guard does nothing. Under the guard of push onto a list of str N (8.5), a text too long is the failure range too, whether or not the list is full.

07-str-guard.pnx

use io .
record entry
  name str 4
end
list rows entry 2
list names str 4 2

def keep v str, r rows do
  v r to entry.name or_else to e args "refused: " v " (" e err_text ")" . cat io.println return end
  args "stored: " r entry.name . cat io.println
end

def main or fail do
  rows add_row or_fail to r
  "four" r keep
  "fourteen" r keep
  args "still: " r entry.name . cat io.println
  "fourteen" names push or_else to e args "push: " e err_text . cat io.println end
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

Output

$ pnx 07-str-guard.pnx
stored: four
refused: fourteen (range)
still: four
push: range

(4b) fits PLACE names a str N place as a store does: record.field, a global (also MODULE.NAME), or an array or a list, for its cells (also a collection parameter, 9.9). It takes the text on top of the stack and gives nothing; it writes nothing. A text of N bytes or fewer goes on; a longer one is the failure range. It is a procedure that can fail, so a guard follows it (11.2 (2)). A program asks a place with it before it does anything a text too long would leave half done, such as taking a row.

07-fits.pnx

use io .
record entry
  name str 4
end
list rows entry 2
array tags str 2 2

def enter v str do
  v fits entry.name or_else to e args "refused: " v " (" e err_text "), rows " rows len . cat io.println return end
  rows add_row or_else to e "full" io.println return end to r
  v r to entry.name
  args "entered: " r entry.name ", rows " rows len . cat io.println
end

"four" enter
"fourteen" enter
"ab" fits tags or_else to e "not reached" io.println end
"abc" fits tags or_else to e args "tags: " e err_text . cat io.println end

Output

$ pnx 07-fits.pnx
entered: four, rows 1
refused: fourteen (range), rows 1
tags: range

(5) A view of bytes made in the region cannot be used once the region is rewound past them; 12.3 states this rule.

7.4 Declared types§

Syntax
type-decl = "type" NAME base ;
base      = "int" | "bool" | "str" | "dec" INT | "proc" effect "end" ;

(1) type meters int makes the declared type meters. Its values are represented like int and cost nothing more to run, but at load it is a different type. It keeps numbers of different units from being mixed.

(2) The name of the type written after a value of the base type makes a value of that type (1500 meters). The procedure raw turns a value of a declared type back into its base type.

(3) Two values of the same declared type can be added and subtracted with add and sub; the result has that type. Comparison procedures and min max also take two values of the same type. Other arithmetic is done after raw.

07-type.pnx

use io .
use str .
type meters int
type seconds int
def pace d meters, t seconds gives int do d raw t raw div end     rem raw: the plain int
1500 meters 300 meters add 300 seconds pace str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 07-type.pnx
6

(2a) type NAME proc signature end declares the type of procedure values that have that signature (type Handler proc n int gives int end). Parameters and locals use the type by its name (h Handler), and ref NAME or def signature do … end gives a value of it (10.5).

(3a) A value of a declared type D over int multiplied by an int (D int mul, int D mul), divided by one or taken modulo one (D int div, D int mod) gives a D. neg and abs give a D too. Scaling a number up or down keeps its unit. The product and the quotient of two D values are not a D, so this rule does not cover them.

07-type-scale.pnx

use io .
use str .
type cents int
def share total cents, people int gives cents do total people div end
def with_tax c cents gives cents do c 110 mul 100 div end
1000 cents 3 share with_tax raw str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 07-type-scale.pnx
366
Constraints

(4) A value of a declared type given where another type goes is refused. Below, the two arguments are swapped.

07-type-mixed.pnx

type meters int
type seconds int
def pace d meters, t seconds gives int do d raw t raw div end
300 seconds 1500 meters pace drop          rem the two arguments are swapped

Refused

$ pnx 07-type-mixed.pnx
07-type-mixed.pnx:4:25: an argument has another type than the procedure's signature asks for

(5) Arithmetic procedures other than add and sub on two values of a declared type are refused. So is any arithmetic procedure outside (3a) on a declared type and an int.

07-type-arith.pnx

type meters int
2 meters 3 meters mul drop

Refused

$ pnx 07-type-arith.pnx
07-type-arith.pnx:2:19: a declared type is added to and subtracted from its own type, and multiplied, divided or taken modulo by an int; for other arithmetic take raw

7.5 Decimals§

Syntax
dec-type = "dec" INT ;   (* 0 to 18 *)
DEC      = [ sign ] digits "." digits ;   (* no exponent: 6.4 *)

(1) A value of dec N is a decimal number with N digits after the point. It is held as an int scaled by 10N: 12.50 is a dec 2 held as 1250. Results are the same on every processor. The range is that of int divided by 10N.

(2) A number with a point and digits on both sides, without an exponent, is a dec N literal whose N is the count of digits after the point: 12.50 is dec 2, 0.5 is dec 1, -0.05 is dec 2.

(3) dec N is a number type over int as a declared type is (7.4): two values of the same dec N are added, subtracted, compared and given to min and max; a dec N is multiplied by an int, divided by one (rounded toward zero, as div) and taken modulo one; neg and abs keep it. In addition dec A dec B mul gives dec A+B, exact, when A+B is at most 18. sum, minimum and maximum (10.6) take rails of dec N and give one. chk_add chk_sub chk_mul chk_div take a dec N as add sub mul div do. An overflow is the fault overflow.

(4) n dec N makes the int n into n with N zeros after the point (5 dec 2 is 5.00); d raw gives the scaled int (12.50 raw is 1250). d M rescale gives d as a dec M, M a constant from 0 to 18: more digits are exact; fewer are rounded half away from zero (2.345 is 2.35, -2.345 is -2.35).

07-dec.pnx

use io .
use str .
type price dec 2
def demo do
  12.50 to unit                           rem dec(2): two digits after the point
  unit 3 mul to three                     rem times an int: still dec(2)
  three 0.75 add to bill
  args "bill " bill ", a quarter " bill 4 div . cat io.println
  0.08 to rate
  bill rate mul to tax                    rem dec(2) times dec(2) is dec(4), exact
  args "tax " tax " -> " tax 2 rescale . cat io.println
  args 5 dec 2 " " bill raw " " 9.99 price raw . cat io.println
  "19.9" 2 str.to_dec or_else to e 0.00 end to read
  args read " " read bill gt . cat io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 07-dec.pnx
bill 38.25, a quarter 9.56
tax 3.0600 -> 3.06
5.00 3825 9.99
19.90 false

07-dec-round.pnx

use io .
def show d dec 3 do args d " -> " d 2 rescale ", " d 0 rescale . cat io.println end
def demo do
  2.344 show  2.345 show  -2.345 show  0.500 show  -0.500 show
end

2.344 -> 2.34, 2
2.345 -> 2.35, 2
-2.345 -> -2.35, -2
0.500 -> 0.50, 1
-0.500 -> -0.50, -1

(5) type price dec 2 declares a type over dec 2; 9.99 price makes one and raw gives the dec 2. dec N is the type of globals, fields (8 bytes), cells of arrays and lists, values of queues and parameters (9.9) as int is. str.to_str and cat write it with all its digits (16.1); str.to_dec reads one.

Constraints

(6) Two dec values of different scales are not added or compared; rescale one first. A dec is not divided by a dec.

def total gives dec 2 do 1.50 0.5 add end      rem dec(2) and dec(1)

07-dec-scales.pnx:1:35: two dec values of different scales: rescale one first (d 2 rescale)

$ pnx 07-dec-div.pnx

7.6 Narrow integers§

(1) u8 u16 u32 u64 i8 i16 i32 are the narrow integer types. The name says the range: u from 0 to 2width−1, i from −2width−1 to 2width−1−1. u8 is the type of a byte and u32 the type of a code point. The 64-bit signed integer is int; there is no type i64.

(2) A narrow integer is another type than int, and each is another type than the others. Conversion is a procedure: n u8 makes the int or other narrow integer n into a u8, and a value outside the range is the fault overflow. Nothing is truncated. A literal is written the same way: 255 u8. A constant outside the range is refused at load. x raw gives the int held; raw of a u64 puts its 64 bits into the int as they are (263 and above are negative). n low_u8 … n low_i32 take the low bits only: these are the truncating procedures.

(3) add sub mul div mod take two of one narrow integer type and give that type; a result outside the range is the fault overflow. wrap_add wrap_sub wrap_mul wrap modulo 2width, sat_add sat_sub sat_mul stop at the ends of the range, and chk_add chk_sub chk_mul chk_div fail. The comparison procedures take two of one type; u64 compares and divides unsigned. neg abs min max clamp do not take them (15.1).

(4) The bit procedures work within the width. bit_not flips the bits of the width only, shl drops the bits that leave the width, and shr keeps the sign of a signed type and fills an unsigned one with zeros. u_shr u_div u_mod u_lt u_le u_gt u_ge floor_div floor_mod are, on an unsigned type, shr div mod lt le gt ge div mod, and do not take a signed type. count_ones leading_zeros trailing_zeros count the bits of the width and give an int (the width for 0); byte_swap reverses the bytes of the width. rotl rotr mul_hi u_mul_hi take u64 only.

(5) A narrow integer is, as int is, the type of globals, of cells of arrays and lists, of values of queues, of parameters and results and of host procedure signatures (19.2), and the base of a declared type (7.4), as in type opcode
u8. A cell of an array, list or queue and a field of a record take the bytes of the width (array a u8 1024 is 1024 bytes); one global is an 8-byte place. A character literal is a u8 or a u32 (6.5). match compares a narrow integer (10.3). A host procedure takes and gives the value as one 64-bit integer, and a result outside the range is the fault overflow (19.2).

07-narrow.pnx

use io .
use str .
def show n int do n str.to_str io.println end
def demo do
  250 u8 5 u8 add raw show               rem 255
  0 u8 1 u8 wrap_sub raw show            rem 255: wraps at 2^8
  200 u8 100 u8 sat_add raw show         rem 255: stops at the end
  200 u8 bit_not raw show                rem 55: eight bits flipped
  -1 low_u8 raw show                     rem 255: the low byte of -1
  0 u64 bit_not 1 u64 gt if "u64 compares unsigned" io.println end
  0 u64 bit_not raw show                 rem -1: the bits as an int
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 07-narrow.pnx
255
255
255
55
255
u64 compares unsigned
-1

fits before a place that is not str Nfits names a place of type str N: record.field, a global, or an array or a list
fits before a localfits names a place a store keeps; a local holds a text of any length
fits before a name that is not declaredfits names a declared global, array or list; there is none of this name
fits with a value that is not strfits takes a text: text fits place
fits with no place after itfits is followed by a place: text fits record.field, or the name of a global

7.7 Floating-point numbers§

Syntax
float-type = "float" ;
FLOAT      = [ sign ] digits [ "." digits ] exponent
           | [ sign ] "0x" hex-digits [ "." hex-digits ] "p" [ sign ] digits ;   (* 6.4 (8) *)
exponent   = "e" [ sign ] digits ;

(1) A value of float is an IEEE 754 binary64 number: a finite number, +0 and -0, the two infinities, and NaN, which means not a number. A value is held in 64 bits.

(2) A float computation does not stop with a fault. A result too large is an infinity (1e300 1e300 f.mul), and a result with no meaning is a NaN (0e0 0e0 f.div, an infinity minus an infinity). A NaN and an infinity pass on into the next computation: a program that does not check carries a NaN to its result. f.is_nan and f.is_finite (16.14) ask whether a value is a NaN and whether it is finite.

(3) A number with an exponent (2.5e0, 1e-3) and a hexadecimal number with p (0x1.8p1) are float literals. A number with a point alone is a dec (7.5). A literal is rounded once to the nearest value, ties to even. A literal too large is an infinity.

(4) The arithmetic is f.add f.sub f.mul f.div of the module f (16.14). The result is the exact value rounded once to the nearest float (ties to even). The arithmetic procedures of int (add neg abs min max and the others, 15.1) take no float, and float, int and dec do not mix in one procedure. n f.from_int makes an int the nearest float; x f.to_int makes a float an int, cut toward zero.

(5) eq ne lt le gt ge compare two float values exactly. -0e0 0e0 eq is true. A NaN is equal to no value, itself included: with a NaN, eq lt le gt ge are false and ne is true. if follows the value of the compare: nan 1e0 lt if … else … end takes the else branch. To compare within a tolerance, use f.near (16.14).

07-float.pnx

use io .
use str .
use f .
def demo do
  1.5e0 2.25e0 f.add to total              rem a float literal has an exponent
  args total " " 1e0 3e0 f.div " " 1e20 " " 0x1.8p1 . cat io.println
  0.1e0 0.2e0 f.add to near_third
  args near_third " " near_third 0.3e0 eq " " near_third 0.3e0 1e-12 f.near . cat io.println
  7 f.from_int 2e0 f.div to half_seven     rem int to float: rounded to the nearest
  args half_seven " " half_seven f.to_int " " -7.9e0 f.to_int . cat io.println
  "2.5e-3" str.to_float or_else to e 0e0 end to read
  args read " " -0e0 " " 0e0 -0e0 eq . cat io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 07-float.pnx
3.75 0.3333333333333333 1e20 3.0
0.30000000000000004 false true
3.5 3 -7
0.0025 -0.0 true

07-float-nan.pnx

use io .
use f .
def demo do
  0e0 0e0 f.div to nan                     rem no fault: the result is a NaN
  1e0 0e0 f.div to inf
  nan 1e0 f.add to still                   rem and the NaN goes on
  args still " " inf " " inf f.neg " " 1e300 1e300 f.mul . cat io.println
  args still f.is_nan " " inf f.is_finite " " nan nan eq " " nan nan ne . cat io.println
  nan 1e0 lt if "lt" else "not lt" end io.println
  nan 1e0 ge if "ge" else "not ge" end io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 07-float-nan.pnx
nan inf -inf inf
true false false true
not lt
not ge

(6) The same computation gives the same bits on every processor. There is one NaN that a computation makes: the quiet NaN with the sign bit 0 (0x7ff8000000000000). The processor does not fuse a product and a sum into one rounding.

(7) Like int, float is the type of globals, cells of arrays and lists (8 bytes), values of queues, locals, parameters and results, the value of a const, a field of a record (8.8), and signatures of host procedures (19.2). A host receives the 64 bits of a double in one integer slot. sort sort_by (15.3) and sum minimum maximum (10.6) take float. An args value (16.13) holds a float too. Types declared over float, keys of indexes and match take no float.

(8) str.to_str and cat write the text with the fewest digits that reads back as the same value, always with a point or an exponent: 1.0, 0.1, 1e20, -0.0. An exponent has no leading zero: 1e6, 1e-7. The infinities are inf and -inf, a NaN is nan. str.to_float (16.1) reads that text.

Constraints

(9) Giving a float and an int or a dec to one procedure, or a float to an arithmetic procedure of int, is refused. A number with a point alone is a dec, so in the place of a float it is refused.

use f .
def f gives float do 1e0 1 f.add end

Refused

$ pnx 07-float-mix.pnx

07-float-int-word.pnx

def f gives float do 1e0 2e0 add end

Refused

$ pnx 07-float-int-word.pnx
07-float-int-word.pnx:1:30: the int procedures take no float; a float is computed with f.add, f.sub, f.mul and f.div

07-float-dec.pnx

def f gives float do 1.5 end

Refused

$ pnx 07-float-dec.pnx
07-float-dec.pnx:1:26: a result has another type than the signature says
Faults

(10) f.to_int stops with the fault overflow when it takes a NaN or a value outside the range of int. No other float computation makes a fault.

07-float-to-int.pnx

use io .
use f .
def whole x float gives int do x f.to_int end
2.5e0 whole drop
"before" io.println
0e0 0e0 f.div whole drop
"never printed" io.println

Diagnostics
ConditionMessage
a float given to an arithmetic procedure of intthe int procedures take no float; a float is computed with f.add, f.sub, f.mul and f.div
a float given to negneg takes an int; a float is negated with f.neg
f.add f.sub f.mul f.div of a value that is not a floatf.add, f.sub, f.mul and f.div take two float values; an int is made a float with f.from_int

8 Declarations§

8.1 General§

Syntax
declaration = [ "export" ] ( [ "bound" ] bindable | "shared" shareable | decl ) ;
bindable    = "global" NAME type
            | "array"  NAME type capacity
            | "buffer" NAME capacity ;
shareable   = bindable
            | "list"   NAME type capacity
            | "index"  NAME NAME PATH ;
decl        = "const"  NAME literal
            | "err"    NAME
            | "list"   NAME type capacity
            | "queue"  NAME type capacity
            | "pool"   NAME NAME capacity
            | "record" NAME { field | "big_endian" } "end"
            | "type"   NAME base
            | "index"  NAME NAME PATH
            | "tasks"  NAME capacity [ size [ size [ size ] ] ] [ "apart" ]
            | "extern" c-name effect "from" STRING [ "as" NAME ] "end"
            | "test"   NAME "do" { body } "end" ;
capacity    = size | "host" ;
size        = INT | NAME ;                         (* NAME: a const *)

(1) A declaration makes a name and what it stands for (a value, storage, a type). Declarations are written only outside definitions, at the outermost level of a source.

(2) A processor reads a source once, from top to bottom. A name shall be declared before the place where it is used. The exceptions are a procedure that calls itself, and forward (8.11).

(3) Within one module a name cannot be made twice, not even for different kinds of things. The names of core procedures and types cannot be made again either.

(4) A capacity (size) is a positive integer literal or a const of one. Capacities are fixed at load and do not change while running. All storage is placed inside the state’s block at load.

(4a) The capacity of an array, a buffer, a list, a queue, a pool or a task group may be written host. Then it is the number the host gave for that declaration before the load (19.4 (1d)), and the load treats it as that number written there. A load that meets host for a declaration the host gave no number is refused, and the message names the declaration. host is a procedure of the declaration only in that place; a constant of that name is not looked up there.

08-host-capacity.pnx

tasks handlers host 32 8192 apart     rem as many as the host serves at once
list seen int host
def count gives n int do seen len end

Refused

$ pnx 08-host-capacity.pnx
08-host-capacity.pnx:1:16: the host gave no capacity for handlers (pinax_capacity)

(5) Globals, cells of arrays, slots of lists, queues and pools, buffers and fields of records start at zero (7 (3)).

Constraints

(6) Making a name that exists already is refused.

08-name-twice.pnx

global total int
const total 5

Refused

$ pnx 08-name-twice.pnx
08-name-twice.pnx:2:7: this name is already defined

(7) Using a name before its declaration is refused.

08-use-before.pnx

use str .
def show gives s str do total str.to_str end
global total int

Refused

$ pnx 08-use-before.pnx
08-use-before.pnx:2:25: this name is not declared before this place

8.2 Constants§

(1) const NAME literal makes a constant. Its type is the literal’s. A constant has no storage: its value goes where it is used. Constants can be capacities, match values and row values.

(1a) The value of an int constant, and the capacity of an array, list, pool, queue or buffer, may be a constant expression: integer literals, the names of earlier int constants and the procedures add sub mul div mod neg abs min max shl shr bit_and bit_or bit_xor, written as in code (the values first), on the line of the first token. It is worked out once, when the source is loaded, so the declaration is a literal to everything after: const cells slots 2 mul. An overflow, a division by zero, a shift outside 0 to 63 and a capacity below 1 are load errors at the expression; an expression that does not leave exactly one value is refused. The size of str N and the count, depth and region of tasks are one literal or one constant name, since more numbers follow them on the line.

08-const-expr.pnx

use io .
use str .
const slots 8
const cells slots 2 mul        rem 16: a size that follows from another, worked out when the source is loaded
const grid slots slots mul 1 sub
array hm int cells
array board int slots 3 mul 1 add
def main do
  cells str.to_str io.println
  grid str.to_str io.println
  hm len str.to_str io.println
  board len str.to_str io.println
end
main

Output

$ pnx 08-const-expr.pnx
16
63
16
25

08-const-expr-overflow.pnx

const twice big 2 mul

Refused

$ pnx 08-const-expr-overflow.pnx
08-const-expr-overflow.pnx:2:19: the constant expression overflows
Constraints

(2) Nothing can be stored into a constant. Inside a definition v to CONST would make a new local of the same name and is refused by the rule against hiding names (9.5); outside a definition to makes no local, so it is refused. set writes globals only (9.4).

08-const-store.pnx

const limit 3
def raise do 4 to limit end

Refused

$ pnx 08-const-store.pnx
08-const-store.pnx:2:19: this name is already visible here; a new name may not hide it

8.3 Globals§

(1) global NAME type makes a global that holds one value. The type is int, bool, err, dec N, str N, a declared type, a row type (the name of a table) or a handle type; not str (7.3).

(2) A global is read by writing its name and stored with v set NAME (9.4). Its value stays as long as the state does — after a procedure’s run ends, and across later loads.

08-const-global.pnx

use io .
use str .
const limit 3
const greeting "hello"
global hits int
global last str 16
global seen bool
hits str.to_str io.println           rem a global starts at zero
limit set hits
greeting set last
true set seen
args last " " hits " " seen . cat io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-const-global.pnx
0
hello 3 true

8.4 Arrays§

Syntax
assign-item = "assign" NAME "(" value { "," value } ")" ;

(1) array NAME type capacity makes an array with that many cells. An array is always full: len is its capacity. The element type is int, bool, err, dec N, str N, a narrow integer (7.6), a declared type, the name of a record, or the name of a table, whose rows the cells then hold (8.8 (5a)). A cell of a narrow integer takes the bytes of its width, a cell of any other value 8 bytes; the cells of lists and queues are the same.

(2) i ARRAY idx reads cell i; v i set ARRAY stores into cell i; a cell of a collection parameter (9.9) is stored the same way. Numbers count from 0. For an array of records idx gives a row (8.8), not a value.

(3) assign ARRAY (value, …) fills an array from cell 0, outside definitions. With fewer values than cells the rest stay as they are. Assigning the same array again starts from cell 0 again. It may be used in a data load (13.4).

(4) The name of an array used as a rail yields its cells from 0 in order (10.6).

08-array.pnx

use io .
use str .
array primes int 6
assign primes (2, 3, 5, 7)                rem cells 4 and 5 stay 0
11 4 set primes                            rem v i to array: store into cell i
primes do to p p str.to_str io.print " " io.print end each
"" io.println
args "len " primes len ", cell 2 is " 2 primes idx . cat io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-array.pnx
2 3 5 7 11 0 
len 6, cell 2 is 5
Constraints

(5) More values in assign than the array has cells is refused.

08-assign-many.pnx

array small int 2
assign small (1, 2, 3)

Refused

$ pnx 08-assign-many.pnx
08-assign-many.pnx:2:21: assign has more values than the array has cells
Faults

(6) An index below 0, or equal to or above the capacity, is the fault range.

08-array-range.pnx

use io .
array primes int 4
"reading cell 4 of 4" io.println
4 primes idx drop

$ pnx 08-array-range.pnx

8.5 Lists§

(1) list NAME type capacity makes a list whose length grows from 0 up to its capacity. Its cells are read and stored like an array’s, but only indexes below the length may be used.

(2) v LIST push adds one value at the end; LIST pop takes the last one off and gives it. Both can fail (or fail): a push into a full list fails with err.full, a pop from an empty list with err.range; a push of text too long for a list of str N fails with err.range (7.3 (4a)). A list of records gets an empty row at the end with LIST add_row, which gives that row. LIST clear sets the length to 0.

08-list.pnx

use io .
use str .
list stack int 3
def fill or fail do
  1 stack push or_fail
  2 stack push or_fail
end
fill or_else to e "fill failed" io.println end
args "len " stack len " of " stack capacity . cat io.println
stack pop or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println
args "len " stack len . cat io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-list.pnx

2
len 1

08-list-full.pnx

use io .
list two int 2
1 two push or_else to e end
2 two push or_else to e end
3 two push or_else to e args "third push failed: " e err_text . cat io.println end

Output

$ pnx 08-list-full.pnx

(2a) n LIST truncate cuts the length to n, for lists of integers, of text and of records alike. It takes back a row added with add_row whose values turn out to be wrong.

08-list-truncate.pnx

use io .
record city
  name str 16
  people int
end
list cities city 4
rem Add a row, and take it back when its values turn out wrong.
def add_city name str, people int or fail do
  cities len to before
  cities add_row or_fail to c
  name c to city.name
  people 0 lt if before cities truncate err.format fail end
  people c to city.people
end
"Seoul" 9411000 add_city or_else to e end
"Nowhere" -1 add_city or_else to e args "refused: " e err_text . cat io.println end
args cities len " rows" . cat io.println

$ pnx 08-list-truncate.pnx

1 rows
Constraints

(2b) A list of records whose rows are kept elsewhere cannot be truncated. It is refused when the same source has a field, a global or a collection that holds its rows, a row of it named with row, or an index of it (8.10): once a new row takes the place cut off, they would point at the wrong row. A row held in a local is checked when it is used (fault range).

  name str 16
end
list cities city 4
index by_name cities city.name
def forget do 0 cities truncate end

$ pnx 08-list-truncate-kept.pnx
08-list-truncate-kept.pnx:6:24: this list's rows are kept by a field, a global, a collection, a named row or an index; it cannot be truncated
Faults

(3) An index past the length is the fault range, even when it is below the capacity. So is a number for truncate larger than the length, or below zero.

1 items push or_else to e end
1 items idx drop                          rem the list holds one value: index 1 is past it

ConditionMessage
truncate on a list whose rows are keptthis list's rows are kept by a field, a global, a collection, a named row or an index; it cannot be truncated

8.6 Queues§

(1) queue NAME type capacity makes a queue: what goes in first comes out first. The element type is int, bool, err or dec N. v QUEUE put puts a value at the back, QUEUE take takes the front one off and gives it, and QUEUE peek gives the front one without taking it. All three can fail: putting into a full queue is err.full, taking from an empty one err.range.

08-queue.pnx

use io .
use str .
queue jobs int 4
def show gives s str or fail do jobs take or_fail str.to_str end
10 jobs put or_else to e end
20 jobs put or_else to e end
jobs peek or_else to e 0 end str.to_str io.println
show or_else to e "?" end io.println
show or_else to e "?" end io.println
show or_else to e args "empty: " e err_text . cat end io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-queue.pnx
10
10
20
empty: range

8.7 Buffers§

(1) buffer NAME capacity makes a buffer of that many bytes: a sequence of bytes that can be changed, for building text piece by piece.

(2) s BUF append, n BUF append_int (decimal; n an int or a narrow integer) and b BUF append_byte (b a u8) add at the end; when there is not enough room they fail with err.full and add nothing. BUF contents gives a str view of what it holds now. n BUF truncate cuts the length to n. BUF clear sets the length to 0.

08-buffer.pnx

use io .
buffer out 32
def build or fail do
  "x=" out append or_fail
  42 out append_int or_fail
  '!' out append_byte or_fail
end
build or_else to e "full" io.println end
out contents io.println
2 out truncate
out contents io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-buffer.pnx
x=42!
x=

(3) The view contents gives points at the buffer’s bytes: when the buffer changes, so do the bytes the view sees.

8.8 Records and rows§

Syntax
record   = "record" NAME { field | "big_endian" } "end" ;
field    = NAME width ;
width    = "u8" | "u16" | "u32" | "u64" | "i8" | "i16" | "i32" | "i64"
         | "int" | "bool" | "float" | "varint" | "dec" INT | "str" size
         | NAME ;                                         (* NAME: a table *)
row-item = [ "export" ] "row" NAME [ NAME ] "(" value { "," value } ")" ;
value    = literal | NAME ;                         (* NAME: a const, a row name, none *)

(1) record NAME … end makes a record type, a sequence of fields, each with a width. An int or i64 field reads as int, a u8 … i32 field as that narrow integer (7.6), a bool field as bool, a float field as float (8 bytes), a dec N field as dec N (8 bytes), a str N field as a str view. A field takes a value of its type only. A field whose type is the name of a table holds a row of that table.

(2) Records are not handled as values. One declares an array, list or pool of records (a table) and handles its rows. A row’s type is named after its table. A row holds a number within the table, and every use checks its range (and, for a pool, its generation, 8.9).

(3) Fields are written as the path RECORD.FIELD: row RECORD.FIELD reads, v row to RECORD.FIELD stores.

(4) row TABLE values… . adds one row to a list, outside definitions. Values go in field order, one after another without commas or parentheses; trailing fields may be left out (they are zero). row TABLE as NAME values… . names the row; the name stands for the row in later row values and in code.

08-record.pnx

use io .
record user
  name str 16
  age u8
  admin bool
end
list users user 8
row users "kim" 30 true .
row users as lee "lee" 25 .                  rem a named row; the fields left out stay zero
def show u users do args u user.name " " u user.age " " u user.admin . cat io.println end
users do to u u show end each
26 u8 lee to user.age                         rem v row to record.field
lee show

Output

$ pnx 08-record.pnx
kim 30 true
lee 25 false
lee 26 false

(4a) A float field holds the 64 bits of a binary64 and starts as 0e0. A row item takes a float literal. The value stored and read is the one the procedures of f compute; a NaN and an infinity are kept as they are.

08-record-float.pnx

use io .
use f .
record point
  x float
  y float
  label str 8
end
list points point 4
row points 1.5e0 -2e0 "a" .
row points as origin .                       rem the fields left out are 0e0 and ""
def length_sq p points gives float do p point.x p point.x f.mul p point.y p point.y f.mul f.add end
def show p points do args p point.label " " p point.x " " p point.y " " p length_sq . cat io.println end
0 points idx show
origin show
0.5e0 origin to point.x  1e300 origin to point.y   rem a float field takes a float only
origin show                                  rem 1e300 squared is an infinity, not a fault

Output

$ pnx 08-record-float.pnx
a 1.5 -2.0 6.25
 0.0 0.0 0.0
 0.5 1e300 inf

(5) A field or global that holds a row starts as “none”. row is_none asks whether it is none, TABLE none gives the none row of that table, and row row_index gives the row’s number.

(5a) An array or a list whose element type is the name of a table holds rows of that table, in cells of 8 bytes: the row’s number plus one, with a pool row’s generation in the upper 32 bits; 0 is none, and every cell starts as none. Its cells are read, stored, pushed, popped and walked as any cells are, and a value going in shall be a row of that table. A row read from a cell is checked where it is used, as any row is. A queue holds no rows. A row that alloc has just given (8.9) is stored into a cell with set, which takes it over as a field does; push refuses it, since a push that fails would lose it.

08-row-cells.pnx

use io .
record city
  name str 12
  people int
end
list cities city 4
list big cities 4                          rem rows of cities
row cities "Oslo" 709 .
row cities "Bergen" 291 .
row cities "Tromso" 78 .
cities do to c c city.people 100 gt end big filter_into or_else to e end
big cities sort_by city.name
big do to c c city.name io.println end each

Output

$ pnx 08-row-cells.pnx
Bergen
Oslo

(6) big_endian sets only the byte order that bytes.pack and bytes.unpack of 16.5 use. It does not change the layout in memory.

Constraints

(7) The values of row shall match the fields in order and type.

08-row-types.pnx

record user
  name str 16
  age u8
end
list users user 8
row users 30 "kim" .

Refused

$ pnx 08-row-types.pnx
08-row-types.pnx:6:11: a value has another type than its field
Faults

(8) An int stored into a narrow integer field is converted first (n u8); a value that does not fit the width makes that conversion the fault overflow (7.6). Nothing is cut: to store the low bits take a procedure such as low_u8. Reading or storing a field of the none row is the fault range.

08-record-narrow.pnx

record pixel
  level u8
end
array image pixel 4
def set_level n int do n u8 0 image idx to pixel.level end     rem the conversion checks the range
300 set_level                                                   rem 300 does not fit in u8

$ pnx 08-record-narrow.pnx
08-record-narrow.pnx:5: integer overflow
  n int = 300

8.9 Pools§

(1) pool NAME RECORD capacity makes a pool of rows that are taken and given back. POOL alloc takes a free row (or fail, err.full when none is left); row POOL free gives it back; row POOL is_alive asks whether the row is still alive.

(2) A row of a pool holds a generation besides its number. Giving a row back changes the generation of its slot, so a row used after it was given back is noticed — even when another row has taken the slot since.

(3) The row alloc gives is an owned value (12.4). On every path it shall be stored exactly once into a field or global, or given to free. Once stored, the generation check guards it.

08-pool.pnx

use io .
record node
  value int
end
pool nodes node 2
global kept nodes
def demo or fail do
  nodes alloc or_fail to a                 rem an owned row: it must be stored or freed
  7 a to node.value
  a set kept                                rem stored: the global holds the row now
  args "value " kept node.value ", alive: " kept nodes is_alive . cat io.println
  kept nodes free
  args "alive after free: " kept nodes is_alive . cat io.println
end
demo or_else to e "no room" io.println end

Output

$ pnx 08-pool.pnx
value 7, alive: true
alive after free: false

(3a) POOL do (r POOL) … end each visits the rows of the pool that are alive, in the order of their slots, not in the order they were taken. A row given back in the block before the walk reaches it is not visited; a row taken in the block is visited when its slot comes later. each is the only combining procedure (10.6) that walks a pool.

Constraints

(4) A path on which a taken row is neither stored nor given back is refused.

  keep nodes free

A combining procedure other than each on a poola pool is walked by each only

8.10 Indexes§

(1) index NAME TABLE RECORD.FIELD makes an index that finds rows of a table of records (an array, a list or a pool) by one field. The key field is int or str N. An index is a hash table of fixed size, matched to the table’s capacity, that holds only row numbers; the data stay in the table.

(2) key INDEX lookup gives the row with that key (or fail, err.not_found when there is none). row INDEX insert puts a row in (or fail; it fails when the key is there already) and row INDEX remove takes it out. To change a key field, remove the row, change it and insert it again.

(2a) key INDEX has gives true when a row with that key is in the index, else false. It does not fail.

(3) Rows written with row at load are in the index. Rows added while running with add_row are found only after insert.

08-index.pnx

use io .
use str .
record user
  name str 16
  age u8
end
list users user 8
index by_name users user.name
row users "kim" 30 .
row users "lee" 25 .
def find_age name str gives age int or fail do name by_name lookup or_fail user.age raw end
"lee" find_age or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println
"park" find_age or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 08-index.pnx
25
-1

use io .
use str .
record user
  name str 16
  age int
end
list users user 4
index by_name users user.name
def add_user name str, age int, indexed bool or fail do
  users add_row or_fail to r
  name r to user.name
  age r to user.age
  indexed if r by_name insert or_fail end  rem a row added while running is indexed by insert
end
def age_of name str gives int or fail do name by_name lookup or_fail user.age end
"kim" 30 true add_user or_else to e end
"lee" 25 false add_user or_else to e end
"kim" age_of or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println
"lee" age_of or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println     rem not inserted: not found

Output

$ pnx 08-index-insert.pnx
30
-1

(3a) The table of an index may be a pool (8.9). Then lookup gives the row as it is now, with its generation; a row given to insert or remove after it was given back is the fault stale. free takes the row out of every index over its pool first. A row alloc has just given is handed over to insert (12.4): when insert fails, the row goes back to the pool before the failure passes on.

08-index-pool.pnx

use io .
record user
  name str 16
  age int
end
pool users user 4
index by_name users user.name
def add_user name str, age int or fail do
  users alloc or_fail to r
  name r to user.name
  age r to user.age
  r by_name insert or_fail                rem hands the row over to the index
end
def forget name str do
  name by_name lookup or_else to e return end to r
  r users free                            rem out of by_name too
end
"kim" 30 add_user or_else to e end
"lee" 25 add_user or_else to e end
"kim" 41 add_user or_else to e args "kim again: " e err_text . cat io.println end
args "kim: " "kim" by_name has ", park: " "park" by_name has . cat io.println
"kim" forget
args "kim after free: " "kim" by_name has . cat io.println
users do to r args r user.name " " r user.age . cat io.println end each

(4) The hash is keyed (SipHash-2-4); the host gives the key (19.2). A host that indexes text from outside should give a random key: whoever knows the key can pile up collisions and make lookups slow.

8.11 Forward declarations§

Syntax
forward = "forward" ( "array" | "list" | "pool" ) NAME
        | "forward" NAME effect "end" ;

(1) forward list NAME announces a table declared further on. It is for a record that holds rows of the table that holds it. The name of an announced table may be used only where a type goes. forward word is in 9.7.

(2) An announced table shall be declared in the same module with the same kind.

8.12 Bound storage§

(1) global, array and buffer with bound in front get their storage from the host. Scripts use them like other globals. Until the host binds them they use room inside the state. 19.7 says how to bind.

8.13 Shared storage§

(1) global, array, list, buffer and index with shared in front only read another state’s storage. The declaring state has no storage for them; the host gives it the same declaration of another state with pinax_share (19.7). Many states may read the same data at once, on many threads, with no copy and no lock.

Constraints

(2) Nothing changes a shared global: storing, set, push, pop, clear, truncate, add_row, storing into a field, insert, remove, the procedures that append to a buffer, and a map_into or filter_into destination are all refused. The processor also refuses, at load, bytecode that changes a shared global, and ends with the fault state bytecode that would change a shared global it was given as a parameter.

record city
  name str 12
  people int
end
shared list cities city 1000
def grow r cities do r city.people 1 add r to city.people end

$ pnx 08-shared-write.pnx

(3) A shared collection may be passed as a collection parameter (9.9) of a procedure that only reads that parameter. A procedure changes its parameter when it uses an instruction that changes it, or passes it to a procedure that changes that parameter or to a host procedure’s buffer parameter. The processor decides once the whole source is read, so the same holds for a procedure announced with forward and for a procedure of an earlier load.

(3a) A shared collection is not passed as a host procedure’s buffer parameter or as a parameter of the procedure a block value names (call), since what the receiver does is not known at load. redefine cannot make a procedure change a parameter it only read.

(4) shared does not stand before queue, pool, tasks, const or record.

Semantics

(5) Until the host gives it, it is empty: lists and arrays have length 0, an index finds nothing, a scalar is 0 and a buffer has no bytes. The code of a load runs as usual. Runs of the host are refused until every shared global is given (19.7).

8.14 Failure codes§

(1) err NAME makes a failure code: a new error code (11.1), of type err. Like a constant (8.2) it has no storage, and its name is a name of its module: another module writes module.NAME, when it is exported. It is used where any code is: with fail, with or_else to e and eq, as a match value, in an err global or collection. err_text gives its name.

(2) The failure codes a state declares are numbered from 0x400 in the order they are declared (19.1). A program does not depend on the number; a host reads the name (pinax_error_text).

08-err.pnx

use io .
use str .
err key_too_long
err value_too_long
def check k str, v str or fail do
  k str.len 8 gt if key_too_long fail end
  v str.len 16 gt if value_too_long fail end
end
def try k str, v str do
  k v check or_else to e
    e match
      when key_too_long do "the key is too long" end
      when value_too_long do "the value is too long" end
      otherwise e err_text end
    end io.println
    return
  end
  "stored" io.println
end
"name" "value" try
"a long key name" "value" try
"name" "a value of thirty bytes, more" try
key_too_long err_text io.println

9 Procedures§

9.1 Definitions§

Syntax
definition = [ "export" ] "def" NAME effect "do" { body } "end" ;
effect     = [ params ] [ "gives" params ] [ "or" "fail" ] ;
params     = param { "," param } ;
param      = [ NAME ] ( type | collection-type ) ;   (* collection-type: 9.9 *)
type       = [ "owned" ] ( NAME [ size ] | "proc" effect "end" ) ;   (* a type NAME ... proc ... end, 7.4 *)

(1) def NAME signature do body end defines a procedure. The signature stands between the name and do, without parentheses. Procedures are defined only outside definitions, at the outermost level of a source; a procedure cannot be defined inside another.

(2) To call a procedure is to write its name in a body. Where it is called, the topmost values of the stack become its inputs, and when it ends its results are in their place. Core procedures, procedures of standard modules and host procedures are called the same way.

9.2 Signatures§

(1) Every procedure has a signature: its inputs, then gives and its results, then or fail if it can fail. A procedure with neither inputs nor results has no signature to write (def reset do … end). Signatures are checked at load: the stack where a procedure is called shall match its inputs, and the stack where its body ends shall match its results.

(2) An input with a name (w int) becomes a local of that name, and the body starts with an empty stack. An input given as a type only (int) stays on the stack when the body starts. Names on the results side are for the reader only and make no locals. An input may also take a collection (9.9).

09-signatures.pnx

use io .
use str .
def area w int, h int gives a int do w h mul end      rem named inputs become locals
def square int gives int do dup mul end               rem a bare type: the value stays on the stack
global total int
def reset do 0 set total end                          rem neither inputs nor results
3 4 area str.to_str io.println
5 square str.to_str io.println
reset

Output

$ pnx 09-signatures.pnx
12
25
Constraints

(3) The inputs of a signature shall be either all named or all bare types.

09-signature-mixed.pnx

def area w int, int gives int do w mul end

Refused

$ pnx 09-signature-mixed.pnx
09-signature-mixed.pnx:1:31: inputs are all named or all bare types, not a mix

(4) Where the body ends (and at every return) the stack shall hold exactly the results, in order and type. More or fewer values are refused.

09-result-missing.pnx

def half n int gives r int do n 2 div drop end

Refused

$ pnx 09-result-missing.pnx
09-result-missing.pnx:1:44: the stack does not hold exactly the results of the signature here

9.3 The stack§

(1) Values passed between procedures lie on the stack. A literal or a name pushes one value; a procedure takes its inputs off and pushes its results. At load a processor knows, at every place of a body, the depth of the stack and the type of each slot.

(2) Only five core procedures rearrange the stack.

ProcedureBefore → afterMeaning
dupa → a aone more of the top
dropa →discard the top
swapa b → b aexchange the top two
overa b → a b aone more of the second, on top
nipa b → bdiscard the second

There are no deeper procedures (rot pick roll depth). When three or more values are involved, use locals.

09-stack-words.pnx

use io .
use str .
def show a int, b int do args a " " b . cat io.println end
1 2 swap show            rem 2 1
1 2 over drop show       rem over copies the second: 1 2 1, drop gives 1 2
1 2 3 nip show           rem nip drops the second: 1 3
4 dup show               rem 4 4

Output

$ pnx 09-stack-words.pnx
2 1
1 2
1 3
4 4

Note

For a reader new to a stack, here is 2 3 add 4 mul one token at a time (the top on the right).

TokenStack after itWhat happened
22A value goes on.
32 3A value goes on.
add5Two values come off; their sum goes on.
45 4A value goes on.
mul20Two values come off; their product goes on.

At load the processor knows the second column of this table (depth and types) at every place in advance. That is why the mistakes of (3) and (3a) show before anything runs.

Constraints

(3) A procedure given fewer values than it takes is refused. The depth of the stack does not change while running.
