09-stack-short.pnx:1:24: the stack does not hold enough values for this procedure

(3a) When the code outside definitions (5.2) ends, at the end of the source, values left on the stack are refused. The stack at the end of a procedure’s body is 9.2′s.

(4) Using a name that is not defined is refused.

9.4 Locals§

Syntax
store = "to" ( NAME | PATH | "(" NAME { "," NAME } ")" ) ;
set   = "set" ( NAME | PATH ) ;

(1) In a body, to NAME takes the top value off and puts it in that name. When the name is new, a local variable of the value’s type is made; later tos shall store the same type. to stores only into locals (and into fields, with to r.FIELD).

(1a) A global is stored with set NAME: v set NAME for a scalar global, v i set NAME for a cell of an array or a list. A global another module exports is set MODULE.NAME. Inside and outside definitions alike. The rule makes the text show whether a store makes a local or changes a global.

(2) to c to b to a stores the top three values one after another. The name written first takes the top value (to takes one name at a time): the reverse of the order in a signature.

09-locals.pnx

use str .
def stats a int, b int, c int gives s str do
  a b add c add to total                rem the first `to` makes a local of that type
  total 3 div to mean
  a b max c max to top
  args "total " total ", mean " mean ", max " top . cat
end
def split3 gives int, int, int do 1 2 3 end
3 9 6 stats io.println
def show3 do split3 to z to y to x args x y z . cat io.println end   rem the rightmost is the top
show3

(3) A local is visible from where it is first stored to the end of the branch, loop or block around it. A local made outside can be stored into inside.

(4) Storing a value of another type into a local is refused.

9.5 No hiding§

(1) A new name (a parameter, a local, the name of a loop) cannot be the same as a name visible there — a procedure, a global, a constant, a type, a local outside. One name means one thing at one place.

Constraints

(2) A parameter or local with the name of a visible name is refused.

$ pnx 09-shadow-word.pnx
09-shadow-word.pnx:1:28: add is a procedure of the language; choose another name

(3) A procedure of the language — a reserved word, a core procedure, a procedure of clause 15 or 16 written without a module, a type — is never a new name: not of a procedure, a declaration, a parameter, a local or a loop. A reserved word is not the name of a field either; another procedure of the language may be, since a field is always written after its record (8.8). The message says which procedure it is.

9.6 Recursion and tail calls§

(1) A procedure may call itself. No forward declaration is needed.

(2) A tail call — a call that is the last thing a procedure does — reuses the caller’s place. Recursion through tail calls does not grow the depth. It needs no mark.

09-recursion.pnx

use io .
use str .
def fact n int gives int do n 1 le if 1 else n n 1 sub fact mul end end
def count_down n int, acc int gives int do            rem a call in tail place reuses the frame
  n 0 eq if acc return end
  n 1 sub acc 1 add count_down
end
20 fact str.to_str io.println
1000000 0 count_down str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 09-recursion.pnx
2432902008176640000
1000000

(3) Calls that are not tail calls pile up; past the depth limit (annex C) they stop with the fault depth.

(1) forward NAME signature end announces a procedure defined further on, for two procedures that call each other.

(2) The definition shall have the announced signature, in the same module; otherwise it is refused.

9.8 Joining text§

Syntax
cat    = "args" { body } "." "cat" ;       (* each body leaves one value; 9.8 *)

(1) args items… . cat joins the items between args and the period into one str. Each item is a procedure or literal that leaves one value, written one after another without commas. A str goes in as it is, an int in decimal, a bool as true or false. Other forms (hexadecimal and so on) are made into a str first by the procedures that make them (16.2).

(2) The result is a view of bytes made in the region (12.2). The number of items is what the text shows; the processor adds up the length first and writes once.

09-cat.pnx

use io .
use fmt .
def show id int, name str, ok bool do args "id=" id " name=" name " ok=" ok " hex=" id fmt.hex . cat io.println end
255 "kim" true show

Output

$ pnx 09-cat.pnx
id=255 name=kim ok=true hex=ff

9.9 Collections as parameters§

Syntax
collection-type = ( "array" | "list" | "queue" ) cell | "buffer" ;
cell            = NAME [ size ] ;   (* int, bool, err, dec N, str N, a record, or a table: its rows *)

(1) An input of type array T, list T or queue T, or of type buffer, takes a collection: the caller writes the collection’s name there (scores total). In the body the parameter is used wherever the name of such a collection goes — l len, i l idx, v l push, v i set l, l do … end each, … end l map_into, q take, s b append and so on. The cells shall be of the type the parameter says: int bool err, dec N and str N with the same N, or a record. The capacity is not part of the type; any capacity is taken, and l capacity gives the one it has.

09-coll-param.pnx

use io .
list scores int 8
list bonus int 8
queue jobs int 4
array grid int 3
def add_range l list int, lo int, hi int do    rem lo, lo + 1, ... up to hi - 1
  lo hi range do to v v l push or_else to e end end each
end
def summary l list int gives str do args l len " of " l capacity ", sum " l sum . cat end
def fill q queue int, n int do 0 n range do to v v q put or_else to e end end each end
def zero a array int do a do to i to v 0 i set a end each_index end
def demo do
  scores 1 4 add_range  bonus 10 12 add_range
  scores summary io.println
  bonus summary io.println
  jobs 3 fill  args "jobs: " jobs len . cat io.println
  7 1 set grid  grid zero  args "grid: " 1 grid idx . cat io.println

10 Control§

Syntax
control = "if" { body } [ "else" { body } ] "end"
        | "loop" { body } "end"
        | "match" { branch } [ "otherwise" { body } "end" ] "end" ;
branch  = "when" case-value { case-value } "do" { body } "end" ;
leave   = ( "break" | "continue" ) [ INT ] "." | "return" ;
block   = "do" { "to" NAME } { body } "end"
        | "def" effect "do" { body } "end"       (* a block value, 10.5 *)
        | "ref" NAME ;

(1) end closes the innermost open construct. The procedures that open one are def forward extern test record do if loop match when otherwise or_else defer. (forward and extern are closed by the end after their signature, and so is type NAME proc … end.) (A text literal and a note remark close on their own tag, 6.3, 6.5.)

(2) At load a processor compares the stacks of all paths. Where paths meet again, the stack shall be the same whichever path was taken. A leaving branch — one that ends with return, fail, break or a loop that never ends — is not compared.

10.1 Branches§

(1) condition if body end takes the bool on top and runs the body when it is true. condition if body else
body end runs the else body when it is false.

(2) The body of an if without else shall leave the stack as it found it. With else, the two bodies shall leave the same stack.

10-if.pnx

use io .
def sign n int gives str do n 0 lt if "negative" else n 0 eq if "zero" else "positive" end end end
-5 sign io.println
0 sign io.println
def warn n int do n 100 gt if "big" io.println end end      rem no else: the branch leaves the stack as it was
500 warn

Output

$ pnx 10-if.pnx
negative
zero
big
Constraints

(3) Two branches that leave different stacks are refused.

10-if-unequal.pnx:1:47: the two branches of this if leave different stacks

10.2 Loops§

(1) loop body end repeats its body. Inside it, these statements leave the loop:

  • break . — leaves the loop and goes on after its end;
  • continue . — skips the rest of the turn and starts the next one;
  • break N . and continue N . — do it to the Nth loop counted from the innermost (N is an integer literal of 1 or more, 1 when left out); the loops in between are left at once.

A condition is written with if: x 0 eq if break . end. A statement ends with a period. Each may be used any number of times, directly in the body of the loop or inside a branch in it (if else match or_else).

(2) One turn shall leave the stack as it found it, and at every place where the loop is left the stack shall be as it was when the loop was entered. A result of a loop is kept in a local.

10-loop.pnx

use io .
use str .
def digits n int gives int do            rem how many decimal digits
  1 to count_
  loop
    n 10 div to n
    n 0 eq if break . end
    count_ 1 add to count_
  end
  count_
end
12345 digits str.to_str io.println
def first_square_over limit int gives int do
  1 to i
  loop
    i i mul limit gt if break . end
    i 1 add to i
  end
  i
end
50 first_square_over str.to_str io.println

(3) A loop has no name. To leave an outer loop, count: break 2 . leaves two loops at once.

use io .
use str .
def find_pair target int gives str do      rem the first a, b in 1..9 with a*b = target
  1 to a
  0 to b
  loop
    1 to b
    loop
      a b mul target eq if break 2 . end       rem leaves both loops at once
      b 1 add to b
      b 9 gt if break . end
    end
    a 1 add to a
    a 9 gt if "none" return end
  end
  args a " x " b . cat
end

  end

10.3 Choosing§

(1) value match when values… do body end … otherwise body end end takes the int, narrow integer (7.6), err or str on top, compares it with the values of the branches and runs the body of the first equal one. A branch starts with when. The values of a branch are literals, consts of this source, error codes (err.range), or a constant or failure code another module exports (module.NAME, 8.14); several values stand after when one after another (no commas, no parentheses), and the do after them opens the body. When no branch matches, the otherwise body runs. Every branch shall leave the same stack.

10-case.pnx

use io .
const quit_code 9
def describe cmd str gives str do
  cmd match
    when "add" do "adds a line" end
    when "rm" "del" do "deletes a line" end
    otherwise "unknown command" end
  end
end
def level n int gives str do
  n match
    when 0 do "off" end
    when 1 do "low" end
    when quit_code do "quit" end
    otherwise "high" end
  end
end
"del" describe io.println
"mv" describe io.println
9 level io.println

Constraints

(2) return is used only inside a definition (a procedure, a block value, a test). In code outside definitions it is refused.

10.5 Blocks§

(1) do … end is a block. A block is given to a combining procedure only (there is no do … end standing by itself); a block value is written with def (def signature do … end, (2a)). A block is used in two ways.

  • An inline block — a block given directly to a combining procedure (10.6). It is expanded in place, so it can read and store the locals around it, and a return inside it leaves the procedure around it.
  • A block value — def signature do … end stored in a local, or given to a parameter of a proc … end type (7.4). It becomes a nameless procedure, called with call. It does not see the locals around it (it captures nothing); it sees globals.

(2) An inline block takes the values the rail yields (and the number of each_index) into locals with to NAME, written one after another right after do. The names are taken from the top down: in do to i to s … end each_index s is the element and i the number (the element is put first, so i is on top). The signature of a block value is that of a procedure definition, and its names become locals.

10-inline-locals.pnx

use io .
use str .
def total_over limit int gives int do
  0 to acc
  1 10 range do to i i limit gt if acc i add to acc end end each   rem the block sees acc and limit
  acc
end

(2a) ref NAME gives a procedure defined with def, of this source or exported by a module in use (ref by_len, ref geo.area), as a value: its type is proc with the procedure’s signature, and call calls it. Any other procedure is given in a block with the block’s signature; inputs given as types only stay on the stack (9.2 (2)), so the block’s body is the procedure alone: def str, str gives bool do str.starts_with end.

(2b) A value of a proc type may also be the cell of an array or a list, a field of a record (so a row of a table or of a pool) or a global (array ops Op 3, ref plus 0 set ops, 3 4 0 ops idx call). It is kept as the number of the procedure plus one, so that a cell nothing was written to holds none: is_none asks it, and calling none is the fault range. A cell cannot hold a procedure of another signature (the refusal is at the write). Such cells are not ordered, summed, compared or used as the key of an index. A container saved before this (version 5 or older) is refused when loaded.

10-proc-cells.pnx

use io .
use str .
type Op proc a int, b int gives int end
def plus a int, b int gives int do a b add end
record Route
  code int
  run Op                           rem a procedure value in a field
end
array ops Op 2
list routes Route 4
global fallback Op
def main or fail do
  ref plus 0 set ops               rem a cell holds the procedure; the other cell stays none
  def int, int gives int do mul end 1 set ops
  3 4 0 ops idx call str.to_str io.println
  3 4 1 ops idx call str.to_str io.println
  routes add_row or_fail to r
  ref plus r to Route.run
  5 6 r Route.run call str.to_str io.println
  fallback is_none if "no fallback yet" io.println end
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

10.6 Rails and combining procedures§

(1) A rail yields values one after another. A rail is not a value: it cannot be stored, and the combining procedure right after it shall take it. Together they make one loop. A rail is a closed rail when its length is known before the walk and the element at any place can be read (range, an array, a list, str.bytes), and an open rail when it is not: the pieces are taken one after another from a source and the walk is made once (str.split, str.lines, str.words, str.chars, ptn.matches, rex.matches, rex.split, csv.fields, a pool). A rail is evaluated lazily: the loop takes one element at a time, in the order of the walk, and the blocks of the adapters run only for the elements that reach them. A walk that ends early (head, head_while, first, any, break) reads and evaluates nothing more, and nothing is stored between the stages. These make rails:

RailElements
the name of an array or listthe cells’ values (rows, for records); a list up to its length. Queues, buffers and indexes are not rails
the name of a poolits live rows, in the order of their slots; for each only (8.9 (3a))
lo hi rangethe ints from lo up to but not including hi
s sep str.split, s str.lines, s str.words, s str.charsstr views (16.1); chars one UTF-8 character each
s str.bytesu8: the bytes (16.1)
s pat ptn.matches, s re rex.matches, s re rex.splitthe parts matched (16.6, 16.7)
s csv.fieldsthe fields (16.9)

(2) The combining procedures are below; the “block” column is what the block takes and gives.

ProcedureBlockResult
each(T)none
each_index(T, i int)none
fold(acc U, T gives U)U; the first value goes before the rail: 0 xs do … end fold
count(T gives bool)int
any all(T gives bool)bool; stops early once the answer is known
first(T gives bool)T or fail; err.not_found when none
sumnoneint (of a rail of dec N, a dec N); an overflow is the fault overflow. Of a rail of float, a float: added from the first to the last, each addition rounded once, with no fault
minimum maximumnoneint or fail (dec N and float likewise); err.not_found for an empty rail. A float is compared in the order of 15.3 (3), and a NaN among the values is the result
map_into(T gives U)a destination after it; or fail
filter_into(T gives bool)a destination after it; or fail
n times()none; no rail, n times

(1a) An adapter takes a rail and gives a rail. skip N drops the first N elements, head N keeps the first N, step N takes every N-th element (the first one first), and rev walks from the last to the first. They apply in the order written and however many there are, the loop is one: scores skip 2 head 3 is the third to the fifth, scores head 3 skip 1 the second and the third. N is code that leaves one int; it ends at a comma, at do, at the next adapter and before sum, minimum or maximum. It is worked out once, before the loop. A negative N (a step of less than 1) is the fault range. step and rev need a closed rail. skip and head also work on an open rail, where they count the pieces as they come; step comes last; a rail takes sixteen of them. each_index does not count along an adapted rail yet. each, fold, count, any, all, first, map_into, filter_into, sum, minimum and maximum take them.

10-rail-adapters.pnx

use io .
use str .
array scores int 8
assign scores (10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80)
def show n int do " " io.print n str.to_str io.print end
0 10 range step 3 do to i i show end each "" io.println          rem 0 3 6 9
scores skip 2 head 3 do to s s show end each "" io.println       rem the third to the fifth
scores head 3 skip 1 do to s s show end each "" io.println       rem the second and the third
scores rev head 3 do to s s show end each "" io.println          rem from the last
0 20 range skip 2 3 add, head 4 step 2 do to i i show end each "" io.println   rem N may be code, ended by a comma
scores skip 1 head 3 sum show "" io.println                      rem 20 + 30 + 40

10-rail-adapter-step.pnx:2:21: step comes last in a chain: nothing follows it

(1b) filter, map, skip_while and head_while take the block written right before them (do to s s 4 gt end filter). The block takes the element and gives a bool (filter keeps the elements for which it is true, skip_while drops them while it is true, head_while ends the walk at the first for which it is false), or, for map, a value of the same type that takes the element’s place. They run inside the loop, once for each element and in the order written, and never for an element an earlier one dropped; so there is one loop, no storage and no call. A block adapter works on any rail, closed or open (str.words, str.lines, …). On a closed rail skip, head, step and rev come before them in a chain; on an open rail they may stand anywhere, and count the pieces that reach them. The name the block gives the element may be the one the final block uses. The block gives a value and leaves no loop: break and continue in it are refused at load (a loop of its own inside the block may use them); drop an element with filter, end the walk with head_while.

The failure ends the loop and is the failure of the procedure each, so it is taken as every failure is: each is followed by or_fail, or_return or or_else. The end of the elements is not a failure. (4) A rail and its combining procedure make one loop, and in the block of each, each_index or times, break . leaves it and continue . goes to the next element: the rail stops and the code after the combining procedure runs. The rules of leaving a loop hold: the stack is as it was when the block began (10.2 (2)), and the block’s deferred code runs (10.7). A break . in a loop inside the block leaves that loop. break N . and continue N . count such blocks and loops alike as levels (10.2 (1)); the operands of the inner blocks leave with them. The blocks of the other combining procedures, which give a result made from every element, are not left early, and are not crossed.

10.7 Deferred code§

Syntax
defer = "defer" { body } "end" ;

(1) defer CODE end writes code that runs when the enclosing block is left. The block is a procedure’s body, a loop’s body (at every turn) or the do block of a combining procedure (at every run). The code runs on every way out of that block: the block’s end, the end of a turn, break, continue, return, or_return, or_fail and fail. Several run in the reverse of the order they are written. They do not run when a fault ends the run (the state closes the handles then, 19.6).

10-defer.pnx

use io .
use str .
buffer trace 256
def say s str do s trace append or_else to e end end
rem Every way out of a block runs its defers, the last written first.
def step n int or fail do
  "open " say
  defer "close " say end
  defer "flush " say end
  n 0 lt if err.range fail end
  "work " say
end
1 step or_else to e end
-1 step or_else to e "(failed) " say end
trace contents str.trim io.println

Output

$ pnx 10-defer.pnx
open work flush close open flush close (failed)

(2) When deferred code gives an owned value (m release, f file.close), the defer takes that value over. It counts as given on every way out of the block, so no failure path needs code of its own to close it. Inside the block the value can still be lent.

def build or fail do
  1 50 range do to i
    mark to m
    defer m release end
    args "row " i ": " i i mul "\n" . cat report append or_fail
  end each
end
build or_else to e args "full: " e err_text . cat io.println end
args "report: " report len " bytes" . cat io.println

$ pnx 10-defer-owned.pnx

10.8 Ends of statements§

(1) A comma or a dot written in code (not inside a signature or an args … .) ends a statement: the code since the last comma or dot. Neither changes the stack, and neither is required: code without them means what it meant before.

(2) A comma waits for nothing: the effects of the statement may still be under way when the next one starts.

(3) A dot is a barrier: every effect begun before it is finished before anything after it. The processor’s part is to call the function the host gave with pinax_on_barrier (19.4 (3)); the host’s part is to write what its host procedures hold back (standard output, a file’s writes) and to wait for what they started in the background. The end of the code of a load and the end of a session line are a dot, also when they end with a fault. In a source loaded as data the two mark statements and call nothing.

(4) An effect whose result the statement needs (a read, a command’s output) is done when it is reached. Between two dots, effects on the same resource keep the order of the program; effects on different resources may overlap. This edition runs every effect in the order of the program; the overlap is the freedom a later edition may use.

11 Failures and faults§

(1) Things go wrong in two ways. A failure is something expected to happen now and then: text that does not read as a number, a full list, a missing key. The caller handles it on the spot. A fault means the program is wrong: an overflow, a division by zero, an index out of range. It ends the run and is reported to the host. A script has no way to catch a fault.

11.1 Error codes§

(1) Failures and faults have an error code, of type err. Codes are named by constants written after err. (no use needed). The procedure err_text gives the name of a code as a str.

ConstantNameMeaning
err.failedfaileda failure in general; a false assert
err.overflowoverflowan integer overflowed
err.div_zerodiv_zerodivision by zero
err.rangerangean index out of range; taking from an empty queue or list
err.fullfulla capacity is used up
err.depthdepththe call depth limit
err.stalestalea row or handle used after it was given back
err.cancelledcancelledthe task was cancelled (clause 14)
err.interruptedinterruptedthe host cut off what was waited for (clause 19)
err.deadlockdeadlockevery task left waits for a queue that nothing can change (14.3)
err.formatformattext or bytes of the wrong form
err.not_foundnot_foundwhat was looked for is not there

The values are those of pinax_err in the host interface (19.1). A program declares codes of its own with err NAME (8.14); err_text gives their names too. Host modules may add codes of their own.

11-errors.pnx

use io .
err.full err_text io.println
err.not_found err_text io.println
err.format err_text io.println

Output

$ pnx 11-errors.pnx
full
not_found

11.2 Failures§

Syntax
guard = "or_fail" | "or_return" | "or_else" [ "(" NAME ")" ] { body } "end" ;

(1) A procedure whose signature ends in or fail can fail. When it fails it has no results, only an error code.

(2) The token right after a call of a procedure that can fail shall be a guard:

GuardWhen the call fails
or_failthis procedure fails too, with the same code; its signature shall have or fail
or_returnthis procedure ends; the stack there shall match its results
or_else … endthe body makes the results in place of the call; or_else to e … end takes the code into the local e, and without to the code stands on the stack when the body starts, so drop it when it is not used; the body may also leave with return, fail, break or continue

When the call succeeds the guard does nothing and the results stay on the stack.

(2a) A store into a str N place may be followed by a guard as well; it then fails with range when the text is too long (7.3 (4a)). After any other store a guard is refused.

(3) code fail makes this procedure fail with that code. Its signature shall have or fail.

11-failure.pnx

use io .
use str .
def parse_port s str gives port int or fail do
  s str.to_int or_fail to n                 rem not a number: fail with the same error
  n 1 lt n 65535 gt or if err.range fail end
  n
end
def show s str do
  s parse_port or_else to e args "bad port " s ": " e err_text . cat io.println return end
  to p
  args "port " p . cat io.println
end
"8080" show
"http" show
"70000" show

11.3 Faults§

(1) A fault ends the run on the spot. It is the return value of the host function that started the run (pinax_run, pinax_load and so on). A fault inside a task also ends the whole run and every task, unless the task’s group is declared apart (14.4). The state remains and takes the next run.

(2) Faults come from:

  • arithmetic overflow (overflow) and division by zero (div_zero) — 7.1, 15.1;
  • an index out of range of an array or list, a match with no matching branch, the none row, text longer than its str N stored with no guard (range) — 7.3, 8, 10.3;
  • a value that does not fit a narrow field (overflow) — 8.8;
  • a region or task space too small (full) — 12.2;
  • the call depth (depth) — 9.6;
  • a row or handle given back (stale) — 8.9, 19.6;
  • a false assert (failed).

(3) What a run that ends with a fault made in the region is rewound. The handles that run opened are closed by the processor, so on a path of faults owned values need no closing by hand. Values already stored in globals, and what host procedures have already done, stay.

(4) A conforming processor reports the kind of a fault and its line. pnx also shows the locals of the procedure the fault happened in.

12 Memory§

12.1 Overview§

(1) All the storage of a state is in the block the host gave (5.1) and is placed at load, apart from memory the host lends and vouches for (12.1 (2)). No storage appears while running. There is no garbage collector, and no value refers to another by address.

(2) Values lie in four kinds of places:

  • declared storage (clause 8): globals, arrays, lists, queues, pools, buffers; their declarations fix their size;
  • slots of the stack and of locals; their depth is fixed at load (9.3);
  • one region for each task (12.2), where the bytes of text made while running go;
  • memory the host gives: bound and shared storage (8.12, 8.13), the strings it passes to a run and those a KEEP_STR host procedure gives (19.3). The host keeps it alive and unchanged while the state reads it.

(3) So the upper bound of the memory a program uses is known at load. Using up the region or a capacity shows as a fault or a failure while running; it never leads the processor to ask for more memory.

12.2 The region and marks§

(1) Procedures that make new bytes — cat, str.upper, the procedures that turn numbers into text and so on — write the result into the region and give a view of it. The region is filled from the front. The procedure region_free gives the number of bytes left.

(2) mark gives the current place in the region as an owned value (type mark). mark release rewinds the region to that place; every byte made after the mark can be used again. A loop that makes much text marks and releases in every turn.

(3) Bytes put into stored text (str N) are copied there, so they survive rewinding the region.

12-region.pnx

use io .
use str .
global kept str 32
def line i int gives str do args "line number " i . cat end
def demo do
  region_free to start
  1 line to a                                 rem a view of 13 new bytes in the region
  a set kept                                   rem stored text: the bytes are copied out
  start region_free sub to one
  mark to m
  2 1000 range do to i i line drop end each
  start region_free sub to many
  m release                                   rem back to the place of the mark
  start region_free sub to after
  args "one line: " one ", 999 lines: " many ", after release: " after . cat io.println
  kept io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 12-region.pnx
one line: 13, 999 lines: 14877, after release: 13
line number 1

(4) A str result the host receives can be used only until the next call on that state. Text the host keeps longer it copies into its own memory (clause 19).

Faults

(5) A region too small is the fault full.

end

12.3 The life of views§

(1) A view into the region cannot be used once its bytes are rewound. A processor checks this at load. Within one body (a procedure, a block value, the code outside definitions) it counts, for each str value, the marks made before it. mark release takes back the values made after that mark.

Constraints

(2) A release while a value it takes back is still on the stack is refused.

  mark to m
  args "a" "b" . cat
  m release
end

(2a) A release in deferred code that runs because the procedure fails (or_fail, fail; 10.7 (1)) does not count the values the procedure leaves on the stack: the procedure ends there, its stack is not read again, and deferred code takes nothing from it (10.7 (4)). The values of the deferred code itself count as in (2), and a local holding a value taken back is as in (3). A failure carries only its code (11.2), so no str leaves the procedure that way.

use io .
use str .
def check w str or fail do
  w str.len 5 gt if err.range fail end
end
def words_of line str or fail do
  loop
    mark to m
    defer m release end
    line str.lower str.words do to w w check or_fail  w io.println end each
    break .
  end
end
"Pinax interprets" words_of or_else to e args "failed: " e err_text . cat io.println end

failed: range

(3) A local holding a value taken back cannot be read until something is stored into it again.

$ pnx 12-release-view.pnx

(4) The check leans to caution. String literals are not in the region and are never taken back. Every other str — views, stored text read back, values procedures give — counts as made where it appears. Where paths meet, a value counts as the latest and a mark as the earliest. So it may refuse a correct program; then keep the value in a str N or move the mark.

(5) Handing an owned mark to a procedure counts as a release there. A procedure that takes a mark counts its str inputs as made after that mark. Two tasks sharing one region are not followed by this check (clause 14).

12.4 Owned values§

(1) owned before a type means an owned value: an open file and other handles, a row taken from a pool, a mark of the region. A processor checks at load that such a value is handed over exactly once on every path.

(2) An owned value is used in two ways:

  • borrowing: giving it to a procedure that takes the type without owned (f file.write); any number of times; the value stays;
  • handing over: giving it to a procedure that takes it owned (f file.close), storing it in a global or field, putting a row just taken into an index over its pool (insert, 8.10 (3a)), or returning it as an owned result; after that the name is empty and cannot be read.

(3) An owned value is put into a local or handed over at once. It cannot be doubled with dup or discarded with drop. It shall be handed over on the paths of failures (or_fail or_return) and at return too.

12-owned-file.pnx

use io .
use file .
def write_note path str or fail do
  path file.open_write or_fail to f            rem an owned file: it must be closed on every path
  "a note" f file.write or_else to e f file.close e fail end
  f file.close
end
def read_note path str gives s str or fail do path file.read_all or_fail end
"note.txt" write_note or_else to e "cannot write" io.println end
"note.txt" read_note or_else to e "cannot read" end io.println

Output

$ pnx 12-owned-file.pnx
a note
Constraints

(4) Using a value again after handing it over is refused.

12-owned-twice.pnx

use file .
def f path str or fail do
  path file.open_read or_fail to h
  h file.close
  h file.close
end

Refused

$ pnx 12-owned-twice.pnx
12-owned-twice.pnx:5:3: this local gave its owned value away; it holds nothing to read

(5) Doubling or discarding an owned value is refused.

12-owned-dup.pnx

use file .
def f path str or fail do
  path file.open_read or_fail dup file.close file.close
end

Refused

$ pnx 12-owned-dup.pnx
12-owned-dup.pnx:3:31: an owned value is kept in a local or given on at once; this procedure would lose it

(6) A single path that does not hand it over is enough to refuse.

12-owned-path.pnx

use file .
def f path str, quick bool or fail do
  path file.open_read or_fail to h
  quick if return end
  h file.close
end

Refused

$ pnx 12-owned-path.pnx
12-owned-path.pnx:4:12: an owned value in a local is not given on every path (close, free or store it)

(7) In a run that ends with a fault, the processor closes the handles that run opened (11.3 (3)).

Diagnostics
ConditionMessage
A value taken back is on the stack at releasea str made after this mark is still on the stack; the release gives its bytes back
Reading a value taken backthis str was made after a mark that was released since; the region may hold other bytes there now
Reading a value handed overthis local gave its owned value away; it holds nothing to read
Doubling or discarding an owned valuean owned value is kept in a local or given on at once; this procedure would lose it
A path that does not hand it overan owned value in a local is not given on every path (close, free or store it)

13 Modules§

13.1 Using a module§

Syntax
import = "use" NAME [ "as" NAME ] ;

(1) One source is one module. The name the host gave when loading the source is the module’s name (pnx uses the file name without .pnx). Standard modules and host modules (13.3) are modules too.

(2) use MODULE . opens that module in this source; from then on its parts are written as the path MODULE.NAME. use MODULE as ALIAS . makes the same module be written ALIAS.NAME. Only core procedures and what this source declares are written as bare names, and the procedures of the modules a search order names (13.5).

(3) A module that is used shall exist already: a standard module, a module the host registered, or a source loaded earlier. When pnx meets use NAME . it first loads NAME.pnx from beside the program file.

13-use.pnx

use io .
use str .
use geometry .
200 50 geometry.area str.to_str io.println
geometry.unit str.to_str io.println
array corners point 2                       rem an exported record is used by its name
3 0 corners idx to point.x
0 corners idx point.x str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 13-use.pnx
100
10
3

13-use-as.pnx

use io .
use str .
use geometry as g .
200 50 g.area str.to_str io.println

Output

$ pnx 13-use-as.pnx
100
Constraints

(4) Using a module that does not exist is refused.

13-unknown-module.pnx

use geometrie .

Refused

$ pnx 13-unknown-module.pnx
13-unknown-module.pnx:1:5: no module of this name is registered or loaded

(5) A procedure of a module written as a bare name is refused, unless a search order names that module (13.5); so is a path into a module that was not opened.

13-bare-name.pnx

use geometry .
200 50 area drop

Refused

$ pnx 13-bare-name.pnx
13-bare-name.pnx:2:8: this name is not declared before this place

13-no-use.pnx

use io .
5 str.to_str io.println

Refused

$ pnx 13-no-use.pnx
13-no-use.pnx:2:3: this path names neither a module in use nor a record

13.2 Exports§

(1) Another source can use only what was declared or defined with export. Procedures, constants and globals are written MODULE.NAME (an exported global is stored with set MODULE.NAME); exported records and types and the row types of tables are written by their name alone.

(2) The module geometry below is the one the examples of 13.1 use. square is not exported.

geometry.pnx

rem A module: only what is marked export is seen by a source that uses it.
export const unit 10
export record point
  x int
  y int
end
def square n int gives int do n n mul end
export def area w int, h int gives int do w h mul unit square div end
Constraints

(3) Using what is not exported is refused.

13-not-exported.pnx

use geometry .
4 geometry.square drop

Refused

$ pnx 13-not-exported.pnx
13-not-exported.pnx:2:3: the module exports nothing of this name

13.3 Standard modules and host modules§

(1) The standard modules come with the processor and are part of the language: str fmt hash encode bytes ptn rex json csv (clause 16). They are seen only after use.

(2) A host module is a set of procedures the host registered. A module the host did not register does not exist. Everything a script can do outside itself (files, clocks, the environment) is a procedure the host registered. pnx registers the standard host modules io file clock random env (clause 17).

(3) err is a set of constants written as paths without use (11.1).

13.4 Data load§

Syntax
data-source = { data-item } ;
data-item   = [ "export" ] ( [ "bound" ] bindable | "const" NAME literal
              | "list" NAME type size | "queue" NAME type size | "pool" NAME NAME size
              | "record" NAME { field | "big_endian" } "end" | "type" NAME base
              | "index" NAME NAME PATH )
            | "forward" ( "array" | "list" | "pool" ) NAME
            | row-item | assign-item
            | data-value [ data-value ] "set" NAME              (* a global, or a cell *)
            | data-value NAME "to" PATH ;                      (* a field of a named row *)
data-value  = literal | NAME ;                      (* NAME: a const or a row name *)

(1) A source the host reads by data load accepts declarations and values only. Procedure definitions, calls, use, extern, test, control, blocks and cat are refused. Such a source therefore cannot run any code. It is for reading settings, data and other text that is not trusted.

(2) A value is stored with value set NAME, a cell with value index set NAME ("192.0.2.1" 0 set allow) and a field of a named row with value ROW to RECORD.FIELD, as in code (8.8, 9.4). Everything a data source declares counts as exported.

13-data-load.c

#include "pinax.h"
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

static pinax_err load(pinax_state *st, const char *name, const char *text) {
    pinax_err err = pinax_load(st, name, (pinax_str){(const unsigned char *)text, strlen(text)}, PINAX_LOAD_DATA);
    if (err != PINAX_OK) {
        pinax_str why = pinax_error_text(st);
        printf("%s refused: %.*s\n", name, (int)why.len, (const char *)why.ptr);
    }
    return err;
}

int main(void) {
    static unsigned char block[1 << 20];
    pinax_config config = {.struct_size = sizeof config};
    pinax_state *st;
    if (pinax_open((pinax_mem){block, sizeof block}, &config, &st) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;

    /* A settings file: declarations and values only. */
    if (load(st, "settings",
             "global port int\n"
             "global name str 16\n"
             "array allow str 16 4\n"
             "8080 set port\n"
             "\"edge\" set name\n"
             "assign allow (\"192.0.2.1\", \"192.0.2.2\")\n") != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    pinax_global g;
    if (pinax_global_find(st, "port", &g) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    printf("port = %lld\n", (long long)*(const int64_t *)g.ptr);

    /* The same mode refuses code: nothing in such a file can run. */
    load(st, "evil", "def boom do 1 0 div drop end\n");
    load(st, "evil2", "global n int\n1 2 add set n\n");
    pinax_close(st);
    return 0;
}

Output

$ ./13-data-load
port = 8080
evil refused: a data source defines no procedures and uses no modules
evil2 refused: a data source calls no procedures; only literals, const names and stores
Diagnostics
ConditionMessage
A module that does not existno module of this name is registered or loaded
A path into a module not opened, or no recordthis path names neither a module in use nor a record
A name not exportedthe module exports nothing of this name
A definition or use in a data loada data source defines no procedures and uses no modules
A call in a data loada data source calls no procedures; only literals, const names and stores

13.5 The search order§

Syntax
order     = "set_order" { order-one } "." | "get_order" ;
order-one = NAME | "get_order" ;

(1) set_order io str . gives the search order: the modules in which a bare name is looked for. Each module named is opened as by use (13.1 (2), (3)); pnx loads a file module beside the program first, as for use. set_order . empties the order. Without a search order, nothing is looked for in a module.

(1a) Inside set_order, get_order stands for the search order as it is at that place: set_order json
get_order . puts json in front of it, set_order get_order csv . behind it. A module that get_order brings again, or that is named again after get_order brought it, keeps its first place.

(2) A bare name in code is looked for in this order, and the first that has it is taken: the locals and parameters; what this source (or session) declares; the core procedures; then the modules of the search order, left to right. So a name of the source and a core procedure keep their meaning whatever the order holds, and a module added to it cannot change code that compiled before. A procedure of a module named like a core procedure (str.len beside len) is written with its path. A path is read as before.

13-order.pnx

use io .
use str .
set_order io .
set_order get_order str .
get_order
"pinax" upper println
def shout s str do args s upper "!" . cat println end
"hello" shout
"abc" str.len 3 eq if "three bytes" println end

Output

$ pnx 13-order.pnx
order: (io, str)
PINAX
HELLO!
three bytes

13-order-core.pnx

set_order str .
def size s str gives int do s len end

Refused

$ pnx 13-order-core.pnx
13-order-core.pnx:2:31: this procedure takes the name of an array, list, queue or buffer; of a str it is str.len

(3) set_order stands at the top level of a source or of a session line, as often as needed. Each one replaces the order from there to the end of the source; a session keeps it for the lines after, until the next one. A procedure takes what its names found when it was compiled.

(3a) get_order alone at the top level tells the search order at that place, written as set_order takes it, order: io str, as a diagnostic with line 0 at config.diag (19.4 (1)), and changes nothing. It speaks when the source is checked: in a file, before any of the file’s code runs.

(4) A name reached through the search order does not count for the rule against hiding names (9.5): a local may have the name of a procedure of a module in the order, and inside that procedure the local is meant.

Constraints

(5) set_order or get_order inside a definition or a block, a search order that names a module twice or more than 16 modules, and one that names a module that does not exist are refused.

Diagnostics
ConditionMessage
set_order inside a definitionset_order stands at the top level, outside definitions and blocks
get_order inside a definitionget_order stands at the top level, or inside set_order
No period, or parentheses or commasset_order is written set_order io str . : no parentheses, no commas, ended by a period
Not a module nameset_order names modules, separated by spaces and ended by a period: set_order io str .
A module named twicethis module is named twice in the order
More than 16an order names at most 16 modules
search (…), not a procedure of the languagesearch is now set_order: set_order io str .

14 Tasks§

Syntax
tasks-decl = "tasks" NAME size [ size [ size [ size ] ] ] [ "apart" ] ;   (* count, call depth, region bytes, turn limit *)

(1) A task is a flow of execution that takes turns with others inside one state. Tasks change only where one gives way on its own (yield, or a host procedure that waits). So even when two tasks use the same global, no other task comes in between two yields of one task. Tasks are not threads: a state runs on one thread at a time (5.1).

(2) tasks NAME count [depth [region [turns]]] declares a task group of up to count tasks. Each task has its own call depth (depth) and its own region (region bytes); left out, they are the processor’s defaults. turns, when it is written, is the group’s turn limit (14.6). The name of the group is the type of the values that refer to its tasks. Written last, apart makes a fault inside one of the group’s tasks end that task only (14.4 (3a)); apart is a procedure of the declaration only in that place.

14.1 Making and running tasks§

(1) block GROUP spawn makes one task from a block value (10.5) that takes and gives nothing, and gives the task (or fail, err.full when there is no free slot). A new task is stopped and has not run yet.

(2) GROUP run_all runs the tasks of the group in turn until all have ended. A task runs until it yields or ends; then the next one goes on.

14-tasks.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 3
def say s str do s io.println end
def demo do
  do "a1" say yield or_return "a2" say yield or_return "a3" say end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  do "b1" say yield or_return "b2" say end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  workers run_all                          rem run every task of the group until all have ended
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-tasks.pnx
a1
b1
a2
b2
a3

(3) TASK resume runs that one task up to its next yield or its end, and gives true when it has ended. TASK is_done asks whether it has ended. The slot of an ended task is used again by spawn.

14-resume.pnx

use io .
use str .
tasks lone 1
def demo do
  do "step 1" io.println yield or_return "step 2" io.println end lone spawn or_else drop return end to t
  0 to turns
  loop t resume if break . end turns 1 add to turns end     rem resume gives true when the task has ended
  args "resumed " turns 1 add " times, done: " t is_done . cat io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-resume.pnx
step 1
step 2
resumed 2 times, done: true

(4) Tasks stay in the state. When a run the host started ends, a stopped task is still there and can go on in the next run.

14-full.pnx

use io .
tasks pair 2
def demo do
  do yield or_return end pair spawn or_else drop return end drop
  do yield or_return end pair spawn or_else drop return end drop
  do end pair spawn or_else to e args "third spawn: " e err_text . cat io.println return end drop
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-full.pnx
third spawn: full

14.2 Yielding§

(1) yield passes the turn to another task. It can fail (or fail): when the task was cancelled it fails with err.cancelled. In the main run, which is not a task, yield does nothing and succeeds at once.

(2) Tasks share data through globals, queues and lists. A full or empty queue is a reason to yield.

14-queue.pnx

use io .
use str .
tasks workers 2
queue jobs int 2
list done int 8
def producer do
  1 to i
  loop
    i 5 gt if break . end
    true to ok
    i jobs put or_else to e false to ok end
    ok if i 1 add to i else yield or_return end   rem a full queue: let the consumer run
  end
end
def consumer do
  0 to got
  loop
    got 5 ge if break . end
    jobs take or_else to e -1 end to v
    v 0 lt if yield or_return else v done push or_else to e end got 1 add to got end
  end
end
def demo do
  ref producer workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  ref consumer workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  workers run_all
end
demo
done do to v v str.to_str io.print " " io.print end each
"" io.println

Output

$ pnx 14-queue.pnx
1 2 3 4 5

(3) Which procedures may yield (directly or in a procedure they call) is known at load. wait_take and wait_put (14.3) yield too. Such procedures cannot be run from inside a host procedure (clause 19).

14.3 Waiting for a queue§

(1) QUEUE wait_take takes the front value of a queue as take does, but while the queue is empty it yields and looks again when its turn comes back. v QUEUE wait_put puts like put, yielding while the queue is full. Both can fail (or fail): a task cancelled while it waits fails with err.cancelled. When the value can be taken or put at once, cancelling is not looked at.

14-queue-wait.pnx

use io .
use str .
tasks workers 2
queue jobs int 1
list done int 8
def producer do
  1 to i
  loop
    i 5 gt if break . end
    i jobs wait_put or_return              rem waits while the queue is full
    i 1 add to i
  end
  -1 jobs wait_put or_return
end
def consumer do
  loop
    jobs wait_take or_return to v          rem waits while the queue is empty
    v 0 lt if break . end
    v done push or_else to e end
  end
end
def demo do
  ref producer workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  ref consumer workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  workers run_all
end
demo
done do to v v str.to_str io.println end each

Output

$ pnx 14-queue-wait.pnx
1
2
3
4
5

(2) A task that waits for a queue does not run again until some queue has changed. When run_all finds that every task left waits for a queue and none waits for the host, nothing can change a queue any more: that is the fault deadlock. Like a fault inside a task of a group without apart (14.4), it ends every task, those of apart groups too. While a task waits for the host, the state waits (PINAX_WAITING) as before; what that task does when it goes on can free the others.

14-deadlock.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 2
queue asks int 1
queue answers int 1
def demo do
  do asks wait_take or_return drop  1 answers wait_put or_return end workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  do answers wait_take or_return drop  1 asks wait_put or_return end workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  workers run_all                          rem each waits for the other: nothing can go
end
demo
"not reached" io.println

Fault

$ pnx 14-deadlock.pnx
14-deadlock.pnx:8: deadlock: waiting for a queue that nothing can change

(3) The main run is not a task and has no one to give its turn to. In the main run, wait_take on an empty queue and wait_put on a full one are the fault deadlock at once.

14-deadlock-main.pnx

use io .
use str .
queue jobs int 2
def demo do
  jobs wait_take or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println   rem the main run is not a task: no one could fill the queue
end
demo

Fault

$ pnx 14-deadlock-main.pnx
14-deadlock-main.pnx:5: deadlock: waiting for a queue that nothing can change

(4) Only these two procedures are watched for a deadlock. Tasks that wait in a loop of their own (loop … yield …
end), or a task resumed by hand with resume, are not; a host that runs such code gives it a budget (19.5).

14.4 Cancelling§

(1) TASK cancel tells a task it is cancelled: its next yield, or its wait for a queue (14.3), fails with err.cancelled. The task takes that failure and ends in its own way. Cancelling does not stop a task by force.

14-cancel.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 1
def demo do
  do
    loop
      "working" io.println
      yield or_else to e args "stopped: " e err_text . cat io.println return end
    end
  end workers spawn or_else drop return end to t
  t resume drop
  t resume drop
  t cancel                                 rem the task's next yield fails with cancelled
  t resume drop
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-cancel.pnx
working
working
stopped: cancelled
Constraints

(2) The block given to spawn is a block value and does not see the locals around it. Values reach a task through globals and queues.

14-spawn-refused.pnx

tasks workers 2
def demo n int do do n drop end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop end

Refused

$ pnx 14-spawn-refused.pnx
14-spawn-refused.pnx:2:22: this name is not declared before this place

(2a) The block of spawn takes nothing and gives nothing. A block with parameters is refused.

14-spawn-block.pnx

tasks workers 2
def start do def n int do n drop end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop end

Refused

$ pnx 14-spawn-block.pnx
14-spawn-block.pnx:2:46: spawn takes a block that takes and gives nothing, and a set of tasks: do ... end workers spawn
Faults

(3) A fault inside a task of a group without apart ends the whole run and every task. The fault goes to the host like a fault of the main run. The state remains and takes the next run.

14-fault.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 2
global zero int
def demo do
  do "task one" io.println yield or_return "task one again" io.println end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  do 1 zero div drop end workers spawn or_else drop return end drop
  workers run_all
end
demo
"not reached" io.println

Fault

$ pnx 14-fault.pnx
task one
14-fault.pnx:6: division by zero

(3a) A fault inside a task of a group declared apart ends that task only. Its slot is free again, and whoever resumed it goes on as after the task’s end: run_all takes the next task, resume gives true. What the task stored until then stays. The run goes on; the host learns of the fault through pinax_task_faults (19.10 (3)).

14-apart.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 3 16 1024 apart
def work n int do args "100 / " n " = " 100 n div . cat io.println end
def demo do
  do 4 work end workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  do 0 work end workers spawn or_else to e return end drop   rem this one divides by zero
  do 5 work end workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  workers run_all
  "the others finished" io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-apart.pnx
100 / 4 = 25
100 / 5 = 20
the others finished

(4) Two tasks using the same region are not followed by the check of 12.3. Each task has a region of its own, so this does not normally happen.

Diagnostics
ConditionMessage
a block with parameters or results given to spawnspawn takes a block that takes and gives nothing, and a set of tasks: do ... end workers spawn
resume, is_done or cancel on a value that is not a taskthis procedure takes a task
run_all on a collection that is not a task group (an array, a list)run_all takes a set of tasks
a tasks count above 4096a set holds at most 4096 tasks
a call depth of a task outside 1 to 4096the call depth of a task is 1 to 4096
a region of a task above 16 MiBthe region of a task is at most 16 MiB
tasks in a data sourcea data source runs no code and declares no tasks
task_tag on a value that is not an inttask_tag takes an int
a turn limit below 1the turn limit of a task is at least 1

14.5 Naming a task§

(1) n task_tag (int gives) gives the running task a tag: an int the host is told with the task’s fault when its group is declared apart (14.4 (3a), 19.10 (3)). A task’s tag is 0 until it gives one; a later task_tag replaces it. In the main run, which is not a task, the procedure does nothing. The tag is a part of the task, and an image keeps it.

(2) A task learns what it serves after spawn, from a queue or a global (14.4 (2)), so it names itself then. A host that gives each request a number tells its tasks the number, and the task gives it as its tag.

14-tag.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 2 16 1024 apart
queue jobs int 4
def work do
  jobs wait_take or_return to n
  n task_tag                     rem the host is told this tag if the task faults
  args "job " n ": " 100 n div . cat io.println
end
def demo do
  4 jobs wait_put or_return  5 jobs wait_put or_return
  ref work workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  ref work workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  workers run_all
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-tag.pnx
job 4: 25
job 5: 20

14.6 Turn limits§

(1) A turn of a task lasts from the moment it gets the run (from run_all or resume) until it yields, waits or ends. A group declared with a turn limit (14 (2)) allows each turn of its tasks at most that many instructions, counted as the budget counts them (19.5): the cost of each check at a back branch or a call, and the bytes scanned. The count starts again at every turn.

(2) A task that runs past its turn limit faults with cancelled at that point. It cannot take the fault as a failure, since nothing there is written to take one. In a group declared apart the task ends alone (14.4 (3a)), and the host is told as of any such fault (19.10 (3a)). In a group without apart the fault ends the run, as any fault inside a task does (14.4 (3)). So a task that loops without yielding is stopped without stopping the others.

14-turns.pnx

use io .
tasks workers 2 16 1024 5000 apart  rem a turn: at most 5000 before the task yields, waits or ends
def stuck do 0 to i loop i 1 add to i end end                      rem never yields
def steady do
  0 to i
  loop i 1 add to i  i 100000 eq if break . end  i 100 mod 0 eq if yield or_return end end
  args "steady counted to " i . cat io.println
end
def demo do
  ref stuck workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  ref steady workers spawn or_else to e return end drop
  workers run_all
  "the stuck task was stopped; the steady one finished" io.println
end
demo

Output

$ pnx 14-turns.pnx
steady counted to 100000
the stuck task was stopped; the steady one finished

(3) The limit and the budget are counted apart. When the budget runs out inside a turn, the run is suspended and the turn goes on with what was left of it when the host resumes the run. What the budget still held then, less than the cost of the check it ran out at, counts against the turn as used. A task another task resumes runs on the turn of the one that resumed it, and counts against it too.

15 Core procedures§

(1) A core procedure is written as a bare name, without use. The tables of this clause write signatures as in 9.2. T means “any one type”; it is a notation for built-in words only. The stack procedures (dup drop swap over nip) are in 9.3 and the combining procedures that take rails in 10.6.

15.1 Integers§

(1) Arithmetic. Overflow and division by zero are faults (11.3).

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
add sub mul(int, int gives int)add, subtract, multiply
div mod(int, int gives int)quotient rounded toward zero and its remainder (sign of the dividend)
floor_div floor_mod(int, int gives int)quotient rounded down and its remainder (sign of the divisor)
neg abs(int gives int)negation, absolute value; overflow for the smallest int
min max(int, int gives int)the smaller, the larger
clamp(n int, lo int, hi int gives int)n brought between lo and hi
rescale(d dec N, M gives dec M)the decimal with M digits after the point (M a constant); fewer digits rounded half away from zero (7.5)

(2) Procedures that treat overflow otherwise.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
wrap_add wrap_sub wrap_mul(int, int gives int)wrap modulo 264
sat_add sat_sub sat_mul(int, int gives int)stop at the edge of the range
chk_add chk_sub chk_mul chk_div(int, int gives int or fail)fail with err.overflow on overflow, err.div_zero on division by zero

(3) Procedures that read numbers as unsigned: the 64 bits as a number from 0 to 264−1.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
u_div u_mod(int, int gives int)unsigned quotient and remainder; division by zero is a fault
u_lt u_le u_gt u_ge(int, int gives bool)unsigned comparison
mul_hi u_mul_hi(int, int gives int)the upper 64 bits of the 128-bit product (signed, unsigned)

(4) Bits. Shift and rotate counts are taken modulo 64 (their low 6 bits). shl does not check for overflow.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
bit_and bit_or bit_xor(int, int gives int)bit by bit
bit_not(int gives int)every bit flipped
shl shr u_shr(n int, k int gives int)left, signed right, right filling with zeros
rotl rotr(n int, k int gives int)rotate
count_ones leading_zeros trailing_zeros(int gives int)the number of 1 bits, of leading and trailing zeros (64 for 0)
byte_swap(int gives int)the eight bytes in reverse order

(5) On a narrow integer (7.6) the procedures above take two of one type and give that type; overflow, wrapping and saturation are judged by that type’s range. The procedures that read numbers as unsigned and floor_div floor_mod are the plain words on an unsigned type and do not take a signed one. The bit procedures work within the width. neg abs min max clamp do not take a narrow integer; rotl rotr mul_hi u_mul_hi take u64 only.

(2) Examples are in clause 8.

(3) c sort puts the cells of an array, or of a list up to its length, in order from the smallest; c sort_desc from the largest. The cells change in place and the procedure gives nothing. The cells shall be int, a narrow integer, dec N, float, bool (false first) or str N, or of a type declared over one of them. float cells go in one total order: -inf, the negative numbers, -0.0, 0.0, the positive numbers, inf, then every NaN last; sort_desc puts the same order the other way, so a NaN comes first; u64 cells are compared unsigned, str N cells in the byte order of str.compare (16.1). A collection parameter (9.9) is sorted the same way. A list or array of records is refused: an index, a field, a global or a named row may keep its rows. Its rows are put in order through a list of their numbers, by (4).

15-sort.pnx

use io .
list marks int 6
list names str 8 4
rem the cells on one line, a blank between two
def show cells list int do
  0 cells len range do to i i 0 gt if " " io.print end  args i cells idx . cat io.print end each
  "" io.println
end
def main or fail do
  7 marks push or_fail  -2 marks push or_fail  12 marks push or_fail  0 marks push or_fail
  marks sort
  marks show
  marks sort_desc
  marks show
  "pear" names push or_fail  "Fig" names push or_fail  "apple" names push or_fail
  names sort
  0 names len range do to i i 0 gt if " " io.print end  i names idx io.print end each
  "" io.println
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

12 7 0 -2

(4) o t sort_by r.f takes o, an array or list of int, each cell the number of a row of t, or of rows of t (8.8 (5a)); t, an array or list of records, or a pool of records when the cells of o are its rows; and the field r.f of the record t holds, written after the procedure as to and set take their name. It puts the cells of o in order of that field of the rows they number, from the smallest; sort_by_desc from the largest. The field shall be of a type the cells of (3) may have. The rows do not move, so indexes and kept rows stay right. A cell that is not a row number of t, or a none row, is the fault range, and a row of a pool given back since is the fault stale, found before any cell moves: o is left as it was. At most one of o and t may be a parameter.

15-sort-by.pnx

use io .
record entry
  term str 8
  count int
end
list terms entry 8
list order int 8
def count_in t str, n int or fail do
  terms add_row or_fail to r
  t r to entry.term
  n r to entry.count
end
def main or fail do
  "to" 4 count_in or_fail  "be" 2 count_in or_fail  "or" 2 count_in or_fail  "not" 1 count_in or_fail  "a" 4 count_in or_fail
  0 terms len range do to i i order push or_fail end each
  order terms sort_by entry.term
  order terms sort_by_desc entry.count       rem by count; the same count stays in byte order
  0 order len range do to i
    i order idx terms idx to r
    args r entry.count " " r entry.term . cat io.println
  end each
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

(5) Both sorts are stable: cells of equal keys keep their order. A sort by several keys is several sorts, the least important key first.

(6) A sort does not fail. A load that sorts gives the program a work area of 8 bytes for each cell of the largest collection it sorts, or, when it sorts a collection parameter, of the largest array or list; the work area counts as a global of the state, and the block must have room for it. A sort of n cells is charged to the budget as n · ⌈log₂ n⌉ instructions (19.5).

16 Standard modules§

(1) The standard modules come with the processor. They are opened with use MODULE . and written MODULE.PROCEDURE (13.1); the module args (16.13) is part of the core and needs no use. Procedures of standard modules cannot reach outside without the host — they use no files, clocks or environment.

(2) Procedures of standard modules make no new storage. Their results are one of:

  • a view of the bytes they were given; nothing is copied;
  • a view of new bytes written in the region (12.2);
  • bytes appended to a buffer the caller gave. Such procedures end in _into or take a buffer, and fail with err.full when there is not enough room.

16.1 str — strings§

(1) The module str works on strings as bytes. Byte positions count from 0. Only the procedures that work on characters (chars char_count is_utf8) read UTF-8. Changing case (upper lower) changes ASCII only.

(2) Where a separator or a part to look for is taken (sep, part), a str or a single character (int, 6.5) may be given.

16.1.1 Looking and cutting§

(3) All results are views of the string given.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
len is_empty(str gives int) (str gives bool)the number of bytes; is it empty
take skip(s str, n int gives str)the first n bytes; what follows them; when short, what there is
take_last skip_last(s str, n int gives str)the last n bytes; what comes before them
slice(s str, start int, n int gives str)n bytes from start; out of range is the fault range
trim trim_left trim_right(str gives str)the view without white space (space, tab, CR, LF) at the ends
cut(s str, sep gives str, str)before and after the first sep; without sep, s and the empty text
try_cut(s str, sep gives str, str or fail)like cut, but err.not_found without sep
span(s str, class int gives str, str)the leading bytes of that class, and the rest

(4) The classes of span are the constants str.digit str.alpha str.alnum str.space str.upper_case str.lower_case str.hex_digit str.punct (ASCII).

16-str-views.pnx

use io .
use str .
def show label str, s str do args label " [" s "]" . cat io.println end
def demo do
  "  key = value  " to line
  "trim" line str.trim show
  "trim_left" line str.trim_left show
  "take 5" "hello, world" 5 str.take show
  "skip 7" "hello, world" 7 str.skip show
  "take_last 5" "hello, world" 5 str.take_last show
  "skip_last 7" "hello, world" 7 str.skip_last show
  "take 99" "short" 99 str.take show                 rem n beyond the end: what is there
  "slice 7 3" "hello, world" 7 3 str.slice show
  "key = value" " = " str.cut to v to k
  "cut, before" k show
  "cut, after" v show
  "a=b=c" '=' str.cut to v2 to k2                    rem the separator may be a character
  "cut at a char" v2 show
  "2026-10-15" str.digit str.span to rest to year
  "span digits" year show
  "span rest" rest show
end
demo

16.1.3 Making new text§

(6) The results are new bytes written in the region; when the region is used up it is the fault full (12.2). The procedures that read numbers can fail.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning

repeat(s str, n int gives str)n copies joined; a negative n is the fault range

to_dec(s str, N gives dec N or fail)read a decimal: a sign, digits, and a point with at most N digits after it (N a constant); more digits, or anything else, err.format

16.1.4 Rails and writing into buffers§

(7) Procedures that make rails (10.6):

  • s sep str.split — the pieces between seps, empty ones included; sep is a str or one byte (a u8 constant, usually a character literal), as for cut and try_cut;
  • s str.words — the pieces between white space, no empty ones;
  • s str.lines — the lines, without their LF or CR LF;
  • s str.bytes — the bytes (u8);
  • s str.chars — one view (str) for each UTF-8 character.

(8) Procedures that write into a buffer:

  • sep buf STEM str.join_into — appends the pieces of the rail joined by sep (or fail). The rail goes last, since the procedure right after a rail shall take it;
  • s old new buf str.replace_into — appends the text with replacements and gives their number (gives n int or fail).

"" io.println
text END
first line
second line
END

"hi" str.bytes do to b b str.to_str io.print " " io.print end each
"" io.println
"가a!" str.chars do to c args "<" c " " c str.len ">" . cat io.print end each
"" io.println
buffer out 64
", " out "x y z" str.words str.join_into or_else to e end
out contents io.println
out clear

16.2 fmt — numbers as text§

(1) cat puts an int in decimal (9.8). Other forms are made into a str by the procedures of the module fmt. There is no small language of formats (such as %08x). Results are written in the region.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
hex bin(n gives str)hexadecimal (lower case), binary; n an int or a narrow integer (7.6): a negative int as 64-bit two’s complement, a narrow integer as the bits of its width
hex_pad(n, width int gives str)hexadecimal filled with leading zeros to width digits; n as for hex
zero_pad(n, width int gives str)decimal filled with leading zeros to width; the sign takes a place; n an int or a narrow integer (a u64 unsigned)
append_hex(n, buf or fail)appends the hexadecimal to a buffer; n as for hex
fixed(x float, n int gives str)the exact value of x in decimal, rounded to n digits after the point (a tie to even), never in the scientific form; n a constant 0 to 18; a NaN and the infinities as nan, inf, -inf

Decimal is str.to_str; decimal appended to a buffer is append_int (15.3). A width of hex_pad or zero_pad below 0 or from 232 up is the fault range; when the region is used up it is the fault full.

16.4 encode — bytes as text§

(1) The procedures of the module encode are all (s str, buf or fail). They append the result to the buffer and fail with err.full when there is not enough room, or err.format when the input has the wrong form.

ProcedureMeaning
base64_encode base64_decodeBase64 of RFC 4648; when decoding, the closing = may be left out

  "a%20b" out encode.url_decode or_fail  "url decoded" show
end

16.5 bytes — binary data§

(1) The module bytes writes numbers and text into a buffer as fixed byte forms, and reads them from bytes. The writing procedures are (value, buf or fail) (err.full when there is not enough room; nothing is written). The reading procedures are (s str gives value, rest str or fail) (err.format when the bytes run short or have the wrong form).

(2)

ProcedureBytes
put_u8 put_u16 put_u32 put_u64
put_i8 put_i16 put_i32 put_i64		a value of the type the name says (7.6; put_i64 an int), least significant byte first
the same names with _bemost significant byte first
get_u8 … get_i64, get_u16_be …their pairs: a value of the type the name says (get_i64 an int)
put_varint get_varintLEB128: the value as an unsigned 64-bit number, 7 bits at a time (a negative takes 10 bytes)
put_str get_stra length (varint), then the bytes

  s1 bytes.get_u16_be or_fail to s2 to b
  s2 bytes.get_varint or_fail to s3 to c
  s3 bytes.get_str or_fail to s4 to d

16.5.1 Records§

(3) row buf bytes.pack appends one row of a record (8.8) to a buffer, field by field in order (or fail). s row bytes.unpack reads the fields from bytes into the row and gives the rest (gives str or fail). row bytes.packed_size is the number of bytes pack would write.

(4) The bytes of a field: an integer width as that width (most significant byte first when the record has big_endian, least significant first otherwise), int as 8 bytes, float as the bits of its binary64 in 8 bytes, bool as 1 byte, varint as LEB128, str N as a length (varint) and the bytes, a field holding a row as the number it holds (varint).

(5) When pack fails the buffer goes back to the length it had before the call. unpack writes into the row only when every field can be read; when it fails the row is unchanged.

16-bytes-pack.pnx

use io .
use bytes .
use encode .
use str .
record item
  id u16
  name str 8
  delta varint
end
record wire
  big_endian
  id u16
  count u32
end
array items item 2
array wires wire 1
buffer out 64
buffer hex 128
def dump do out contents hex encode.hex_encode or_else to e end  hex contents io.println  hex clear end
def demo or fail do
  0 items idx to a
  513 u16 a to item.id  "pinax" a to item.name  -3 a to item.delta
  a out bytes.pack or_fail
  dump
  args "packed_size " a bytes.packed_size ", written " out contents str.len . cat io.println
  1 items idx to b
  out contents b bytes.unpack or_fail to rest
  args b item.id " " b item.name " " b item.delta ", rest " rest str.len . cat io.println
  "\x01\x02\x05" b bytes.unpack or_else to e args "short input: " e err_text . cat io.println "" end drop
  args "the row is unchanged: " b item.name . cat io.println
  out clear
  0 wires idx to w
  258 u16 w to wire.id  7 u32 w to wire.count
  w out bytes.pack or_fail
  dump
end
demo or_else to e e err_text io.println end

513 pinax -3, rest 0

16.6 ptn — small patterns§

(1) The module ptn finds and replaces text with patterns of the size of Lua’s. It has no alternation (|), no repetition of groups and no back references; rex (16.7) takes the larger grammar.

16.6.1 The text of a pattern§

(2) A pattern is a sequence of the items below, matched byte by byte.

ItemMatches
an ordinary characterthat byte
.any byte
%a %d %l %u %s %w %x %p %cletters, digits, lower case, upper case, white space, letters or digits, hexadecimal digits, punctuation, control characters (ASCII); in upper case, everything else
% and a character that is not a letter or digitthat byte itself (%. %% %()
[…] [^…]a set and its complement, with a-z ranges and % classes inside; a ] right after [ or [^ is a member
* + - ? after an itemzero or more (longest), one or more (longest), zero or more (shortest), zero or one
( … )a capture; up to nine
^ first, $ lastanchored at the start, at the end of the text

16-ptn-classes.pnx

use io .
use ptn .
"a1 B2_c3!" "%a" "." ptn.replace io.println     rem letters
"a1 B2_c3!" "%d" "." ptn.replace io.println     rem digits
"a1 B2_c3!" "%W" "." ptn.replace io.println     rem not letter or digit
"a1 B2_c3!" "[%u_]" "." ptn.replace io.println  rem a set: upper case or _
"aaab" "a-b" "<%0>" ptn.replace io.println      rem - is the shortest repetition
"color colour" "colou?r" "#" ptn.replace io.println

Output

$ pnx 16-ptn-classes.pnx
.1 .2_.3!
a. B._c.!
a1.B2.c3.
a1 .2.c3!
<aaab>
# #

16.6.2 Procedures§

(3)

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
is_match(s str, pat gives bool)is there a match anywhere
match(s str, pat gives str or fail)a view of the first match; err.not_found when none
capture(n int gives str)capture n (1–9) of the last match; 0 is the whole match
matchesrailthe matches in order, each search starting where the last ended
replace(s str, pat, rep str gives str)new text with every match replaced by rep; in rep, %0–%9 are captures and %% is %

(4) A pattern that begins with ^ is tried at the start only, so matches and replace match at most once.

(5) The last match capture reads belongs to each run (task) separately; another match changes it. A run the host starts begins with no match: the match of an earlier run is not seen, since its captures are views of text that run matched, which may be gone.

16-ptn.pnx

use io .
use ptn .
const date "(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)"
def yes b bool gives str do b if "true" else "false" end end
"abc 123" "%d+" ptn.is_match yes io.println
def demo do
  "on 2026-10-15 ok" date ptn.match or_else to e "?" end io.println    rem the whole match
  args 1 ptn.capture "/" 2 ptn.capture "/" 3 ptn.capture . cat io.println
  "key = value" "^(%w+)%s*=%s*(%w+)$" ptn.match or_else to e "?" end drop
  args 2 ptn.capture " <- " 1 ptn.capture . cat io.println
end
demo
"x=1, y=22, z=333" "%a=%d+" ptn.matches do to m args "[" m "]" . cat io.print end each
"" io.println
"2026-10-15" date "%3.%2.%1 (%0)" ptn.replace io.println
"  trim me  " "^%s*(.-)%s*$" "%1" ptn.replace io.println
"aaa" "^a" "-" ptn.replace io.println              rem ^ anchors: one match, at the start

value <- key
[x=1][y=22][z=333]

trim me
-aa
Constraints

(6) A pattern shall be a string literal or a const of one, so that it is checked at load. To search with text made while running, use rex.compile (16.7).
