16.7 rex — regular expressions§

(1) The module rex finds and replaces with regular expressions. Its matching never goes back, so the time it takes is bounded by the length of the text times the size of the pattern. Write patterns as raw strings (6.5): in an ordinary string "\d" is refused as an unknown escape, and "\b" becomes a backspace.

(2) In a source that has use rex the type name regex is visible. A regex value is a pattern program that cannot be changed once made. It is used only in locals, arguments and results.

16.7.1 The text of a pattern§

(3)

FormMeaning
a characterits bytes; a multi-byte character, its byte sequence
.one UTF-8 character; without (?s) not a line break
[abc] [a-z] [^…]a set; ranges are ASCII; a complemented set takes one UTF-8 character
\d \w \s \D \W \Sdigits, word characters, white space and their complements (ASCII)
* + ? {n} {n,} {n,m}repetition (longest); with ? after it, shortest
a|balternation; the left first
( … ) (?: … )a group that captures, one that does not
^ $the start and end of the text; with (?m), of each line
\b \Ba word boundary and its complement (ASCII)
\n \t \r \f \v \0 \xNNthat byte
\ and any other characterthat character (\. \* \\)
\zs \zethe match is narrowed to start, end here; the whole pattern must still match
(?i) (?m) (?s)at the very start of a pattern only: ignore case (ASCII), anchors per line, . also matches a line break

There are no back references, lookaround, Unicode properties or named groups.

(4) A pattern that repeats a body able to match the empty text (such as (a*)*) may give other captures than Perl or Python.

16.7.2 Procedures§

(5) re is a regex value. “The match” is the range narrowed by \zs and \ze.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
rx(pat gives regex)makes the program at load; pat is a literal or a const
compile(pat str gives regex or fail)makes it while running; a malformed pattern is err.format; the program lies in the region
is_match(s str, re gives bool)is there a match
match(s str, re gives str or fail)the first match; err.not_found when none
cut_match(s str, re gives str, str, str or fail)what is before the first match, the match, and what is after
matchesrailthe matches in order; the block takes the whole match and one str parameter per group
splitrailthe pieces between the matches
with_match(s str, re, block or fail)runs the block once with the first match; err.not_found when none
replace(s str, re, rep str gives str)new text with every match replaced; in rep, \0–\9 are groups
replace_into(s str, re, rep str, buf gives int or fail)appends the replaced text to a buffer and gives the number of replacements
replace_by(s str, re, buf, block gives int or fail)appends to a buffer, each match replaced by the text the block gives

(6) When matches, split and replace search again from the next place, they still see the whole text, so ^ and \b know the bytes before that place.

16-rex.pnx

use io .
use str .
use rex .
const pair r"(\w+)=(\d+)"
def yes b bool gives str do b if "true" else "false" end end
def total line str gives n int do               rem groups arrive as block parameters
  0 to n
  line pair rex.rx rex.matches do to value to key to whole
    n value str.to_int or_else drop 0 end add to n
  end each
  n
end
def demo do
  args "sum " "id=7, x=20; name=kim, n=3" total . cat io.println
  "abc 123" r"\d+" rex.rx rex.is_match yes io.println
  "on 2026-10-15 ok" r"(\d+)-(\d+)" rex.rx rex.match or_else to e "?" end io.println
  "key: value" r":\s*" rex.rx rex.cut_match or_else to e "" "" "" end to after to m to before
  args "[" before "|" m "|" after "]" . cat io.println
  "from 2026-10-13 to 2026-11-02" r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})" rex.rx r"\3/\2/\1" rex.replace io.println
  "a , b;c ,d" r"\s*[,;]\s*" rex.rx rex.split do to part args "<" part ">" . cat io.print end each
  "" io.println
  "가나다" r"." rex.rx rex.matches do to ch args "<" ch ">" . cat io.print end each   rem . is one UTF-8 character
  "" io.println
  "foobar" r"foo\zsbar" rex.rx rex.match or_else to e "?" end io.println              rem \zs: the match starts here
  "Hello" r"(?i)HELLO" rex.rx rex.is_match yes io.println
end
demo

16.8 json — JSON§

(1) The module json reads and writes JSON (RFC 8259) text in one direction, without building a tree: it reads one token at a time and writes straight into a buffer.

16.8.1 Reading§

(2) s json.next reads the first token of s and gives (kind int, value str, rest str) (or fail). At the end it fails with err.not_found; on something that is not a token, with err.format. White space, commas and colons between tokens are passed over. The structure of the grammar — matching brackets, where commas go — is not checked.

(3) kind is one of the constants below. The value of a string is its text without the quotes; when it has escapes, they are decoded into text written in the region. The value of a number is its text as written.

ConstantToken
json.object json.object_end{ }
json.array json.array_end[ ]
json.keya string followed by a colon
json.stringany other string
json.numbera number
json.boolean json.nulltrue false, null

(4) s json.skip passes over one value (with everything inside, for an object or array) and gives the rest (gives str or fail).

16-json-read.pnx

use io .
use json .
def kind_name k int gives str do                    rem the kinds are constants of json
  k json.key eq if "key" return end
  k json.string eq if "string" return end
  k json.number eq if "number" return end
  k json.boolean eq if "boolean" return end
  k json.null eq if "null" return end
  k json.object eq k json.array eq or if "open" return end
  "close"
end
def tokens s str do
  s to rest
  loop
    rest json.next or_else to e break . end to rest to value to kind
    args kind kind_name " " value . cat io.println
  end
end
text END
{"name": "kim", "tags": [1, -2.5e3, true, null], "note": "café"}
END
tokens

close }

16.8.2 Writing§

(5) The writing procedures all append to a buffer and fail with err.full when there is not enough room. They put the commas in themselves.

ProcedureSignature
begin_object end_object begin_array end_array put_null(buf or fail)
put_key put_str(s str, buf or fail); the procedure does the escaping
put_int(n int, buf or fail)
put_dec(d dec N, buf or fail)
put_float(x float, buf or fail); the shortest text that reads back. JSON has no NaN and no infinity: err.range
put_bool(b bool, buf or fail)

16-json-write.pnx

use io .
use json .
buffer out 128
def demo or fail do
  out json.begin_object or_fail
  "name" out json.put_key or_fail  "kim \"k\"" out json.put_str or_fail
  "tags" out json.put_key or_fail
  out json.begin_array or_fail  1 out json.put_int or_fail  true out json.put_bool or_fail  out json.put_null or_fail
  out json.end_array or_fail
  out json.end_object or_fail
end
demo or_else to e e err_text io.println end
out contents io.println

16.8.3 Path, validity and layout§

(5a) Four more procedures read the text as a whole, with the strict grammar of RFC 8259 (the token reader above is lenient on purpose: it reads a stream). A text is valid when it is one value and white space; a nesting deeper than 64 is not valid here. A path names a value: names joined by dots, an index in brackets, and a name that holds a dot or a bracket as ["a.b"] (user.langs[1], [0].id); the empty path names the whole text. A name is compared with the key as it is after its escapes are decoded. The reading stops where it finds the value, so the procedures do not check the rest of the text.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
valid(s str gives bool)whether s is one JSON value, with only white space around it
at(path str, s str gives kind int, value str or fail)the value path names in s: its kind (the constants above, never json.key) and its text, as json.next gives it, except that an object or an array is given whole, as written, to be read again by json.next or json.at. err.not_found when there is no such value (a name missing, an index past the end, a name asked of an array or an index of an object); err.format when the path is malformed or the text is malformed where it was read
items members(s str gives rail)rails over the elements of an array, the members of an object (5b)
items_at members_at(path str, s str gives rail)the same for the array or object path names (5b)
minify(s str, b buffer or fail)appends s without the white space between its tokens; err.format when s is not valid, err.full when it does not fit (the buffer is then as it was)
pretty(s str, indent int, b buffer or fail)appends s with each member and element on a line of its own, indent blanks (0 to 16; any other number is a fault) to a level, ": " after a key; an empty object or array stays as it is. The failures are those of minify

16-json-path.pnx

use io .
use json .
buffer shown 512
def main or fail do
  text END
{"user": {"name": "kim", "langs": ["ko", "en"], "age": 31}, "ok": true}
END
  to doc
  doc json.valid to fine
  args "valid: " fine . cat io.println
  "user.name" doc json.at or_fail io.println drop     rem a value by its path: the text, and its kind
  "user.langs[1]" doc json.at or_fail io.println drop
  "user.langs" doc json.at or_fail to langs drop      rem an array is given as written, to be read again
  "[0]" langs json.at or_fail io.println drop
  "user.size" doc json.at or_else to e args "no value: " e err_text . cat io.println 0 "" end drop drop
  doc 2 shown json.pretty or_fail                     rem laid out, two blanks to a level
  shown contents io.println
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

Output

$ pnx 16-json-path.pnx
valid: true
kim
en
ko
no value: not_found
{
  "user": {
    "name": "kim",
    "langs": [
      "ko",
      "en"
    ],
    "age": 31
  },
  "ok": true
}

(5b) Rails (10.6): s json.items walks the elements of the array s and s json.members the members of the object s; path s json.items_at and path s json.members_at walk the array or object the path names (a procedure has one signature, so the path has procedures of its own). Each turn gives the next element as the values (kind int, value str) for an element and (key str, kind int, value str) for a member; the block of each binds them the last pushed first (do to v to k, do to v to k to key). The kind and the value are those of json.next, except that an object or an array is given whole, as written, to be walked again. A text that is not an array (an object) at the place is err.format, a path that names nothing is err.not_found; a text that is damaged after some good elements fails with err.format at the turn that reaches the damage. The walk reads the text once, and a walk that ends early reads no further. A rail that can fail is taken by each and is followed by a guard (or_fail, or_return, or_else); no defer is written in its block.

16-json-rails.pnx

use io .
use str .
use json .
def total s str gives int or fail do                  rem the numbers of an array; the others are passed over
  0 to acc
  s json.items do to v to k
    k json.number eq if v str.to_int or_fail acc add to acc end
  end each or_fail
  acc
end
def show s str or fail do
  s json.members do to v to k to key                   rem the last pushed first: the value, the kind, the key
    args key " (" k ") = " v . cat io.println
  end each or_fail
end
"[1, 2, \"x\", 3, [4, 5]]" total or_else to e -1 end str.to_str io.println
"{\"a\": 1, \"b\": [1,2], \"c\": {\"d\": null}}" show or_else to e "bad" io.println end
def langs s str or fail do                             rem a path names the array
  "user.langs" s json.items_at do to v to k v io.println end each or_fail
end
"{\"user\": {\"langs\": [\"lua\", \"c\"]}}" langs or_else to e "bad" io.println end
"[1, 2" total or_else to e e err_text io.println 0 end drop      rem damaged after two good elements
"[1,2,3,4,5]" json.items head 2 do to v to k v io.println end each or_else to e end   rem lazy: the text is read no further

b (3) = [1,2]
c (1) = {"d": null}

format

16.8.4 Records§

(6) row buf json.pack appends a row of a record as an object whose keys are the field names. s row
json.unpack reads an object into the fields of the same names and gives the rest after the object. Values of unknown keys are passed over. Numbers shall be integers that fit the field’s width; a dec N field takes a number with at most N digits after the point and is written with all N (7.5); a float field takes any number, read as the nearest float, and is written as the shortest text that reads back (7.7). JSON has no NaN and no infinity: pack of a row that holds one fails with err.range and the buffer is left as it was. null is not accepted. The row is written only when everything is right; when it fails (err.format) the row is unchanged.

16-json-record.pnx

use io .
use json .
record user
  name str 8
  id u16
  admin bool
end
list users user 4
buffer out 128
def input gives str do
  text END
{"id": 9, "extra": {"x": [1, 2]}, "name": "park", "admin": false} and more
END
end
def demo or fail do
  users add_row or_fail to u
  "lee" u to user.name  7 u16 u to user.id  true u to user.admin
  u out json.pack or_fail
  out contents io.println
  users add_row or_fail to v
  input v json.unpack or_fail to rest                  rem unknown keys are skipped
  args v user.name " " v user.id " " v user.admin " /" rest "/" . cat io.println
  "{\"id\": 70000}" v json.unpack or_else to e args "70000 in u16: " e err_text . cat io.println "" end drop
  args "the row is unchanged: " v user.id . cat io.println
end
demo or_else to e e err_text io.println end

park 9 false / and more/
70000 in u16: format
the row is unchanged: 9

16.9 csv — CSV§

(1) The module csv reads and writes CSV in the form of RFC 4180: fields are separated by commas; a field that holds a comma, a quote or a line break is quoted, and quotes inside it are doubled.

(2) s csv.fields is a rail (10.6) of the fields of one line. A quoted field is given without its quotes and with doubled quotes made single. An unclosed quote gives the rest of the text as the last field (a rail cannot report a failure).

(3) The writing procedures append to a buffer (or fail, err.full when there is not enough room). s buf csv.put, n buf csv.put_int, d buf csv.put_dec, x buf csv.put_float (nan, inf and -inf too) and b buf csv.put_bool append one field (with the comma it needs); buf csv.end_line ends the line. Booleans are written true and false.

(4) row buf csv.pack appends one row of a record as one line. s row csv.unpack reads one line into the fields in order and gives what follows the line. The row is written only when every field is right (err.format). A dec N field and a float field are read and written as in json (16.8), except that a NaN and the infinities of a float are written nan, inf and -inf and read back.

16-csv.pnx

use io .
use csv .
record user
  name str 8
  id u16
  admin bool
end
list users user 4
buffer out 128
"a,\"b,c\",\"d\"\"e\",,f" csv.fields do to x args "[" x "]" . cat io.print end each
"" io.println
def demo or fail do
  users add_row or_fail to u
  "lee, jr" u to user.name  7 u16 u to user.id  true u to user.admin
  u out csv.pack or_fail                               rem a line, quoted where needed
  "x" out csv.put or_fail  5 out csv.put_int or_fail  false out csv.put_bool or_fail  out csv.end_line or_fail
  out contents io.print
  users add_row or_fail to v
  "zed,5,true\nrest" v csv.unpack or_fail to rest
  args v user.name " " v user.id " " v user.admin " [" rest "]" . cat io.println
  "zed,5,maybe" v csv.unpack or_else to e args "bad bool: " e err_text . cat io.println "" end drop
end
demo or_else to e e err_text io.println end

x,5,false
zed 5 true [rest]
bad bool: format

16.10 sheet — a book of tables of rows and columns§

(1) The module sheet keeps tables of rows and columns, called sheets, in a buffer (8.7) the program declares: the buffer holds a book. It is a library, not a type, and it works as an adapter does: the program opens the book, makes sheets in it, chooses one by name or by number, and every other procedure then works on that current sheet. Every procedure of sheet takes the buffer, written last, as a collection parameter (9.9) does. A cell holds nothing, an int, a bool, a dec N, a float, a date (Unix seconds, UTC) or a str, whatever the program puts there. The kind of a cell is known only to the module: a value leaves a cell through the procedure of its type (int, str, …), so every procedure has a fixed signature and the stack never holds a value of no type. How the cells, the pools and the indexes lie in the buffer is not part of the interface.

(2) Rows, columns and sheets are counted from 0. A row is added at the end by add_row and a sheet holds at most the rmax rows create was given. The number of columns is fixed by create; widen changes it. A value put in a cell is copied. Equal values are kept once, in a pool the whole book shares: a number that does not fit a cell, and every text, go to the pool with a count of the cells that hold them (in any sheet), and a cell that is overwritten, cleared or cut off gives its value back. A pool that has no room is err.full; free text space that is scattered is gathered when a new text needs it (and by compact). sheet is for tables that are read and written by index and by what they hold. What is found by a name is kept in an index (8.10).

16.10.1 Books and sheets§

(3) A procedure other than the ones of this group needs a current sheet: without one it is the fault state. The first sheet made in a book is the current one. A name is 1 to 255 bytes and is kept once in the book. A sheet number is the order in which it was made; the number of a dropped sheet is given again to the next sheet made.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
open_book(nmax int, b buffer or fail)formats the buffer as a book of at most nmax (1 to 256) sheets, with none made; err.full when the buffer is too small. The buffer then reads as full: nothing can be appended over a book
create create_cols(name str, rmax int, cols int, b buffer gives int or fail)makes a sheet of at most rmax rows and exactly cols columns and gives its number. create_cols stores the sheet column by column: a scan of one column is several times faster, reading a whole row is slower. err.format when the name is taken; err.full when there is no room or number left
activate activate_n(name str, b buffer or fail) (n int, b buffer or fail)makes the sheet of that name, or that number, the current one; err.not_found when there is none. A read-only book cannot change its current sheet
current sheets(b buffer gives int)the number of the current sheet (-1 when there is none); one more than the highest number in use
sheet_name(n int, b buffer gives str or fail)a view of the name of sheet n, good until the next write to the book; err.not_found for a number not in use
find_sheet(name str, b buffer gives int or fail)the number of the sheet of that name; err.not_found otherwise
remove(name str, b buffer or fail)removes a sheet with its indexes and gives back what its cells held. When it was the current sheet there is none afterwards
rename(n int, name str, b buffer or fail)gives sheet n another name; err.format when the name is taken
copy_to(row1 int, col1 int, n int, row2 int, col2 int, b buffer or fail)copies a cell of the current sheet into a cell of sheet n, sharing the value; err.not_found when there is no sheet n

16.10.2 Making and growing§

(4) The procedures of this group work on the current sheet.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
rows cols rows_max(b buffer gives int)the rows now, the columns, the most rows
add_row(b buffer gives int or fail)adds an empty row and gives its number; err.full at rmax
truncate_rows(n int, b buffer)keeps the first n rows and gives back what the others held; more than there are is the fault range
widen(cols int, b buffer or fail)makes the sheet again with cols columns, keeping the rows, the values and the indexes. More columns need room in the book (err.full); fewer columns only when the cut columns are all empty (err.format). The old room is left as a hole that compact closes
clear(b buffer)removes every row
compact(b buffer)gathers the free space of the texts and closes the holes between the sheets

16.10.3 Cells§

(5) Procedures that take a row and a column fault with range when the cell is outside the table. A buffer that is not a table is the same fault.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
put_int put_bool(v int, row int, col int, b buffer or fail) (v bool, row int, col int, b buffer or fail)puts a copy in the cell; err.full when a pool is full
put_date(secs int, row int, col int, b buffer or fail)puts a date, the Unix seconds secs (UTC), in the cell; a value that does not fit 60 bits (any date of the years 1 to 9999 does) is the fault range
put_dec(v dec N, row int, col int, b buffer or fail)puts a decimal with its scale
put_float(x float, row int, col int, b buffer or fail)puts a float; a NaN or an infinity, which no file of a sheet holds, is err.range (the cell is left as it was)
put_str(s str, row int, col int, b buffer or fail)puts a copy of the text; a view of this table may be given
clear_cell(row int, col int, b buffer)makes the cell empty
copy_cell(row1 int, col1 int, row2 int, col2 int, b buffer)copies a cell to another, sharing the value
int bool(row int, col int, b buffer gives int or fail) (... gives bool or fail)the value; err.format when the cell holds another kind (a date too: it is read with date)
date(row int, col int, b buffer gives int or fail)the Unix seconds of a date cell; err.format when the cell holds another kind
dec(row int, col int, N int, b buffer gives dec N or fail)a decimal with the scale N (a constant 0 to 18); err.format when the cell holds another kind or scale
float(row int, col int, b buffer gives float or fail)the value of a float cell; err.format for another kind
str(row int, col int, b buffer gives str or fail)a view of the text in the table, good until the next write to it; err.format for another kind
kind is_empty(row int, col int, b buffer gives int) (... gives bool)the kind (sheet.k_empty 0, k_int 1, k_bool 2, k_dec 3, k_str 4, k_date 5, k_float 6); is it empty

16.10.4 Finding and choosing§

(6) A search compares numbers as numbers and texts by what they say. It looks at one column going down, or at one row going across. A text that is in no cell is found to be so at once.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
find_row_int find_row_str(key int, col int, b buffer gives int or fail) (key str, col int, ...)the first row whose column col holds key; err.not_found otherwise. This is MATCH of a spreadsheet; a date cell is found by its seconds, as where_int, narrow_int and the index treat it, and sum_* too; the value is then read with int, str, date, … (there is no procedure that gives a value of no type, as VLOOKUP does)
find_col_int find_col_str(key int, row int, b buffer gives int or fail)the first column of row row, across
find_row_from_int find_row_from_str find_col_from_int find_col_from_str(key, line int, from int, b buffer gives int or fail)the same, starting at row or column from

(7) A sheet keeps a selection: a list of rows, at first all of them. where_* starts again from all the rows and keeps those whose column holds a value in the relation op with v (sheet.eq ne lt le gt ge); narrow_* keeps, of the rows now selected, those that are. Cells of another kind, and empty ones, are never in the relation. Because each procedure works on the selection of the sheet, a line of them is a pipe. The selection is kept in the book, per sheet.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
where_int narrow_int(col int, op int, v int, b buffer)selects, or narrows, by a number
where_str narrow_str(col int, op int, v str, b buffer)selects, or narrows, by a text (byte order)
select_all(b buffer)selects every row
sel_len(b buffer gives int)how many rows are selected
sel_row(k int, b buffer gives int)the row number of the k-th selected row; out of range is the fault range
order_by order_by_desc(col int, b buffer or fail)puts the selected rows in order of column col, smallest (largest) first, stably; numbers (int and dates, a date as its seconds), then texts, then the rest (bool, dec, float, empty). Room for the numbers is taken from the free end of the buffer (err.full)

(8) The totals look at the int and date cells only (a date counts as its seconds). sum_* is the fault overflow when the sum does not fit; min_* and max_* fail with err.not_found when there is no number.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
sum_col min_col max_col count_col(col int, b buffer gives int)over column col, all rows; min and max or fail
sum_row min_row max_row count_row(row int, b buffer gives int)over row row, all columns
sum_sel min_sel max_sel count_sel(col int, b buffer gives int)over column col of the selected rows

16.10.5 Ordered indexes§

(9) A column can have an index: an ordered structure over its numbers and texts (numbers first, then texts by bytes, ties by row), a B+tree of pages taken from the free end of the book. index builds it, writes to the column keep it in step, unindex frees its pages. With an index find_row_* (down the column), where_* with every relation but ne, and order_by with every row selected answer without scanning, in time that grows with the logarithm of the rows and the number of rows found; the answers are the same as without it, rows in row order. An index costs a write, and a book whose pages and sheets fill the buffer refuses a new one with err.full; a write that would need a page that is not there is err.full too and changes nothing. The index is a means, never a meaning: a program that does not use it works as before.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
index(col int, b buffer or fail)builds the index of column col of the current sheet (nothing when there is one); err.full when the book has no pages left
unindex(col int, b buffer)removes it
indexed(col int, b buffer gives bool)whether the column has one

16.10.6 Files§

(9a) CSV and xlsx files are read into the current sheet and written from it, without any power over files: the program reads the file into a buffer (file.read_all_into) and writes the buffer out (file.write of contents). These procedures take two buffers, the file first and the book last (0 blob book sheet.load_csv); the two are different buffers, and a name for the file may be a collection parameter (9.9) while the book is a buffer of its own. A procedure that takes the file may change the bytes of its buffer: it is a work area (a shared buffer is refused). A load adds rows after the last row of the current sheet and gives the number added; when it fails, the sheet is as it was. Rows beyond rows_max or columns beyond the sheet are err.full, a text that is not a CSV or a file that is not an xlsx is err.format. The mode is 0, 1 or 2 (any other is a fault).

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
load_csv(mode int, f buffer, b buffer gives n int or fail)reads the text in f: lines end with LF or CRLF, fields with commas, a quoted field holds commas, line breaks and doubled quotes (it is unescaped in place), blank lines and a UTF-8 BOM are skipped. Mode 0: a field that is an integer in its canonical form (-?(0|[1-9][0-9]*), fitting an int) becomes an int; a canonical integer with 1 to 18 digits after the point, fitting, becomes a dec of that many digits (1.50 is dec 2); an empty field is an empty cell; any other, 007 and -0 too, is text. Mode 2: as mode 0, and a field that is a date, YYYY-MM-DD, or with T or a blank and hh:mm:ss (and perhaps a Z), that exists, becomes a date cell (UTC; a date alone is midnight). Mode 1: all text
load_xlsx(mode int, n int, f buffer, b buffer gives rows int or fail)reads sheet n (0 first, in the order of the workbook; err.not_found when there is none) of the xlsx in f. Numbers follow the CSV rule (the digits after the point beyond 18 are rounded; an exponent is applied; a value that does not fit is text), shared, inline and formula-result strings are text (rich text is joined, phonetic runs dropped), t="b" is a bool, an error value (#N/A) is text, a formula gives its stored result. A cell whose number format is a date or time (built-in formats 14 to 22, 27 to 36, 45 to 47, 50 to 58, 71 to 81, or a custom format with y, d, h, s or m outside quotes and brackets, [h] and [mm] included) is, in mode 0, an int of Unix seconds (UTC, the 1900 or 1904 date system of the file, a time of day alone counted from midnight); in mode 1 it stays the serial number as a dec, in mode 2 it is a date cell with those seconds (the other cells as in mode 0). Rows and columns the file leaves out are empty cells
save_csv(dst buffer, b buffer gives n int or fail)replaces the contents of dst with the current sheet as CSV (up to its last used row and column; texts quoted when they hold a comma, a quote or a line break; dec with its digits; float as the shortest text that reads back; bool as true and false; a date as YYYY-MM-DD, with Thh:mm:ss when it is not midnight, and outside the years 0 to 9999 as its seconds) and gives the bytes; err.full when dst is too small (it is then empty)
save_xlsx(dst buffer, b buffer gives n int or fail)replaces the contents of dst with an xlsx of the current sheet (one sheet, named like it, at most 31 characters without []:*?/\; texts as inline strings; numbers, dec, float and bool as such; a date as an Excel date, the serial number of the 1900 system with the format yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss (a styles part is written only for a sheet that has one), read back by mode 2 with the same seconds; before 1900-03-01 or after 9999-12-31 the format cannot say it and the seconds are written as a plain number). The ZIP is stored, not compressed

(9b) work area: nothing is allocated (clause 12). load_xlsx uses the spare capacity of the buffer that holds the file after its last byte, about 130 KB (a window for the inflate, the scanner’s buffers) plus the decoded shared strings (4 bytes for each and their text). The buffer is declared larger than the file; when the room does not suffice the load is err.full. A part of the file is read through the central directory of the ZIP: ZIP64, encrypted parts and methods other than stored and deflate are err.format, as is a part larger than 256 MiB when inflated. Every byte inflated is charged to the instruction budget.

16-sheet-files.pnx

use io .
use csv .
use sheet .
buffer book 65536
buffer blob 262144
def fill or fail do
  "name" blob csv.put or_fail  "qty" blob csv.put or_fail  "price" blob csv.put or_fail  blob csv.end_line or_fail
  "a, \"b\"" blob csv.put or_fail  7 blob csv.put_int or_fail  "1.50" blob csv.put or_fail  blob csv.end_line or_fail
  "007" blob csv.put or_fail  "" blob csv.put or_fail  "-2" blob csv.put or_fail  blob csv.end_line or_fail
end
def main or fail do
  1 book sheet.open_book or_fail
  "t" 20 3 book sheet.create or_fail drop
  fill or_fail                                       rem in a program the file is read by file.read_all_into
  0 blob book sheet.load_csv or_fail to n            rem mode 0: numbers become numbers, "007" stays text
  args "rows " n ", row 1 column 1 is " 1 1 book sheet.kind ", row 2 column 0 is " 2 0 book sheet.str or_fail . cat io.println
  blob book sheet.save_xlsx or_fail drop             rem the book written as an xlsx into the same buffer
  1 book sheet.open_book or_fail
  "back" 20 3 book sheet.create or_fail drop
  0 0 blob book sheet.load_xlsx or_fail to m         rem and read from it: mode 0, workbook sheet 0
  args "read back " m " rows, price is a dec: " 1 2 book sheet.kind sheet.k_dec eq . cat io.println
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

16.11 toml — TOML§

(1) The module toml reads TOML text of version 1, a file of settings, without building a tree. A value is given as the bytes it has in the text, and a string without its quotes; a string with escapes, or of several lines with a backslash at the end of a line, is decoded into text written in the region (12.2). Nothing is converted: a number is given as written (5_000, 0xff), to be read by the program with the procedure of the type it wants. The module can also change a file (below), keeping every byte it does not change.

(2) kind is one of the constants below.

ConstantValue
toml.tablea header [a.b], or a table a path names: no value
toml.tablesa header [[a.b]] of an array of tables: no value
toml.stringa string of any of the four kinds
toml.int toml.floata number as written; inf and nan are floats
toml.booltrue or false
toml.datetimea date, a time or both, as written (1979-05-27T07:32:00Z)
toml.array toml.inlinean array or an inline table whole, as written, to be read again by toml.at

16.11.1 Reading§

(3) s toml.next reads the first statement of s and gives (kind int, key str, value str, rest str) (or fail): a header (kind toml.table or toml.tables, key the name between the brackets as written, value empty) or a pair (key as written, dots and quotes included, value as above). Blank lines and comments are passed over. At the end it fails with err.not_found; a statement that is not TOML is err.format. The program keeps the header it is under; every key is relative to it.

(4) path s toml.at gives (kind int, value str) (or fail): the value path names, in the way a reader of the file would see it. A path is names joined by dots (a quoted name, "a.b" or 'a.b', may hold dots) and indexes in brackets: server.ports[1], user[0].name, a."b c".d. Keys given with dots (a.b.c = 1), tables made by a header, inline tables and arrays are all followed, and an index chooses an element of an array of values or of tables (the order of the [[...]] headers; those below an element belong to it). A path that names a table gives toml.table and no value. err.not_found when there is none; err.format when the path is malformed or the text is malformed where it was read. The text of a toml.float value is read as a float by str.to_float (16.1), except that an _ between digits (1_000.5) is not read: err.format. A float is written by giving its str.to_str text and the kind toml.float to toml.set (7); nan, inf and -inf are TOML values too.

16-toml-float.pnx

use io .
use str .
use toml .
use f .
buffer out 128
def show path str, doc str or fail do
  path doc toml.at or_fail to v to k
  v str.to_float or_else to e args path ": " v " is not read: " e err_text . cat io.println return end to x
  args path ": " x . cat io.println
end
def demo or fail do
  "pi = 3.1415\nfar = +inf\nbig = 1_000.5\n" to doc
  "pi" doc show or_fail  "far" doc show or_fail  "big" doc show or_fail
  "pi" doc 0e0 0e0 f.div str.to_str toml.float out toml.set or_fail    rem a float written back
  out contents io.print
end
demo or_else to e e err_text io.println end

Output

$ pnx 16-toml-float.pnx
pi: 3.1415
far: inf
big: 1_000.5 is not read: format
pi = nan
far = +inf
big = 1_000.5

(5) s toml.valid gives whether every statement of s is well formed. The check is of the syntax of each statement: a key given twice, a table defined twice and the range of a number or the existence of a date are not checked by it.

(6) s toml.check (or fail) checks the rules of the whole document as well: a key is defined once, a table once (a table made by a header may be named again only as the parent of one already made), a table made by dotted keys is not opened again by a header, an inline table and an array are closed (nothing is added to them later), and an array of tables is not also a table. Every integer must fit 64 bits signed, every float must be finite, and a date or time must exist (the month and the day of that year, hours to 23, minutes to 59, seconds to 60; seconds are required, as in TOML 1). err.format when a rule is broken or a statement is malformed; err.full when the region has no room for the table the check keeps (at most one node for each byte of s; it is given back when the procedure ends), never “valid”. A name written with escapes is the same key as the same name written bare, and a part with escapes longer than 256 bytes is err.full.

(7) path s value kind b toml.set (or fail) appends to b the text s with the value of path set: the value of a key that is there is replaced (an element of an array too), the comments and the layout stay. A key that is not there is added at the end of the statements of its table (the root table: before the first header), dotted from there when the path goes through tables that are not yet there (server.tls.on = 1); a table that exists only through the headers of tables below it gets a header of its own at the end of the text. kind is toml.string (value is the text, written quoted and escaped; it must be UTF-8), toml.int, toml.float, toml.bool or toml.datetime (value is the text of one, as the language writes it, and a number out of range or a date that does not exist is refused), or toml.array (value is an array on one line). Another kind, a table as a path, a path under a value, and an index beyond an array of tables are not written: err.format, except an index of an array of tables that is not there, which is err.not_found. The text s and the result must keep the rules of toml.check, else err.format; err.full when the buffer has no room, and the buffer is then as it was.

(8) path s b toml.remove (or fail) appends to b the text s without the statement of the key path names, from the start of its line to the end of it (a comment on that line goes with it). err.not_found when there is none; err.format for a table, for an element of an array or of an inline table (they are not statements of their own), or when the text is malformed; err.full as for toml.set.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
valid(s str gives bool)whether every statement of s is well formed
check(s str gives or fail)the rules of the whole document; err.format, err.full
at(path str, s str gives kind int, value str or fail)the value path names in s; err.not_found, err.format
items(s str gives rail)a rail over the statements of s (10)
next(s str gives kind int, key str, value str, rest str or fail)the first statement of s and what is left after it; err.not_found at the end, err.format
set(path str, s str, value str, kind int, b buffer or fail)appends s with the value of path set; the rules above
remove(path str, s str, b buffer or fail)appends s without the statement of the key path

use io .
use toml .
def main or fail do
  text END
title = "Pinax"          # a comment
[server]
host = "localhost"
ports = [8080, 8081]
[[user]]
name = "kim"
[[user]]
name = "lee"
END
  to conf
  "title" conf toml.at or_fail io.println drop       rem the text of a string, without its quotes
  "server.ports[1]" conf toml.at or_fail io.println drop
  "user[1].name" conf toml.at or_fail io.println drop
  "server" conf toml.at or_fail drop toml.table eq to is_table
  args "server is a table: " is_table . cat io.println
  conf to rest                                        rem every statement, in order
  loop
    rest toml.next or_else to e break . end to rest to value to key to kind
    args kind " " key " [" value "]" . cat io.println
  end
end
main or_else to e e err_text io.println end

(10) s toml.items is a rail (10.6) over the statements of s: each turn gives (kind int, key str, value str) as toml.next does, and the block of each binds them the last pushed first (do to v to k to kind). A statement that is damaged fails with err.format at its turn, after the good ones; like every rail that can fail it is taken by each and followed by a guard.

  out contents io.println
end

16.12 md — Markdown§

(1) The module md reads Markdown, a text for people, and writes it as HTML. It is a subset of CommonMark with the tables and the strikethrough of GFM, made for the notes, the READMEs and the pages a script meets; it is not every corner of the specification. Raw HTML in the text is never passed on: < is written as &lt;. A link or an image whose address has a scheme other than http, https, mailto, tel and ftp is written as its text only. So the HTML is safe to put in a page whatever the Markdown was.

(2) What is read. Blocks: ATX headings (# to ######) and setext headings, paragraphs, thematic breaks, block quotes, lists (bullets - + *, numbers 1. 1), nested, tight or loose), fenced code (three or more backticks or tildes, the first word of the info string becoming class="language-..." when it is letters, digits and - _ + # .), indented code, and tables (a row, a row of dashes with colons for the alignment, rows). Inline: emphasis *a* _a_, strong **a** __a__, strikethrough ~~a~~, code spans, links [text](address "title"), images ![alt](address), autolinks <https://...> and <a@b.c>, backslash escapes, character references (&amp; &#65;), a hard break (two blanks or a backslash at the end of a line). Not read: link reference definitions, raw HTML, a setext heading after a list, and the finer rules of CommonMark for emphasis next to punctuation; these give text or a plain paragraph, never a failure. A nesting of containers or of emphasis deeper than 12 is written as text. The search for the closing mark of a link, an emphasis or a code span is paid from a budget of sixteen bytes for each byte of the text; when it is spent, the marks left are text, so a text that is all unclosed marks is read in a time that grows with its size.

16.12.1 Writing HTML§

(3) s b md.html appends the HTML of the Markdown text s to the buffer b, s b md.inline that of one line or paragraph, with no block around it. They fail with err.full when there is not enough room (the buffer is then as it was). The room is needed for the HTML itself and, while a block quote or a list item is written, for a copy of it at the end of the buffer, one for each level the block lies in, none longer than the text. s is not the buffer.

16.12.2 Reading by blocks§

(4) s md.next reads the first block of s and gives (kind int, level int, text str, rest str) (or fail); at the end it fails with err.not_found. Nothing is copied: text is a view of s. kind is one of the constants below, text what the table says, and level the level of a heading (1 to 6), 1 for an ordered list and 0 for the others.

Constanttext
md.headingthe text of the heading, without its # and its underline, to be read as inline Markdown
md.paragraphthe lines of the paragraph, as written
md.codefenced: the lines between the fences; indented: the lines as written, with their indentation
md.quote md.list md.tablethe block as written, with its markers, to be given to md.html
md.ruleempty

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
html(s str, b buffer or fail)appends the HTML of the Markdown text s; err.full
inline(s str, b buffer or fail)appends the HTML of the text of one line or paragraph; err.full
blocks(s str gives rail)a rail over the blocks of s (6)
next(s str gives kind int, level int, text str, rest str or fail)the first block of s and what is left after it; err.not_found at the end

16.13 args — values of mixed kinds§

Syntax
args-value = "args" { body } "." ;              (* each body leaves one value, 9.8 *)
param      = NAME "args" ;                      (* a parameter that takes an args value *)

(1) The module args and the type args are part of the core: unlike the other modules of this clause, the procedures of args are written args.WORD without a use. An args value holds a number of values of different kinds, and a procedure that takes a varying number of values takes one of them, in a parameter NAME args (def show label str, rest args gives str do … end).

(2) args v1 v2 … . makes an args value of the values that the code between args and the period leaves; each item leaves one value. The values are int, bool, str, dec N or float; a number of another type, a record or a collection is not one of them. An args holds from 1 to 64 values. The values are copied into the region (12.2): a str is copied with its bytes, so the args value does not depend on where the text was. Written right before cat, the values are not built: args a b . cat joins them as 9.8 says.

(3) An args value has a life down the calls only: it is a parameter. It is not stored in a local or a global, not given back as a result and not a value of another args. It goes on to any procedure that takes an args (rest inner), and rest cat writes its values as args … . cat writes them: a str as it is, an int in decimal, a bool as true or false, a dec N with all its N digits, a float as str.to_str writes it (7.7).

16.14 f — floating-point computation§

(1) The module f holds the procedures of float (7.7); use f . opens it. The four arithmetic procedures round the exact value once to the nearest float (ties to even). No procedure makes a fault (f.to_int excepted): a NaN and an infinity pass on as results (7.7 (2)).

from_int(n int gives float)the float nearest to n (ties to even)
to_int(a float gives int)the int cut toward zero; the fault overflow for a NaN or a value out of range

17 Standard host modules§

(1) The modules of this clause are host procedures that come with the processor. They are not part of the language: they exist only when a host registers them (13.3). pnx registers all seven. A host that embeds the library picks them one by one with pinax_host_register(state, "io") and the like (library libpinax_host). Using a module that was not registered is refused (13.1).

(2) Host procedures keep the same rules as other procedures: their signatures are checked at load, procedures with or fail shall be guarded, and owned values are handed over exactly once.

(3) What the operating system refuses is a failure (or fail). A missing file and the end of an input are err.not_found, bytes of the wrong form err.format, no room err.full, and any other refusal (permission, a device gone) err.failed. A procedure without or fail (print, close) does not report the operating system’s refusal.

17.1 io — standard input and output§

(1)

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
print println(s str)writes to standard output; println adds a line break (LF)
eprint(s str)writes to standard error
read_line(gives line str or fail)one line of standard input, without its line break; err.not_found at the end of input
read_line_into(buf buffer or fail)appends one line to a buffer

Bytes are written unchanged; the same bytes come out on every operating system.

17.4 Channels and the host loop§

(1) A channel is a line of byte messages, up to a set number of them. The host names a channel and registers it in a state as a module of that name (pinax_channel_register, library libpinax_host). The states that registered the same channel pass messages to each other. They share no memory: a message is copied in and copied out.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
send(msg str or fail)puts a message in; waits while the channel is full
receive(gives msg str or fail)takes the message that came first; waits while it is empty
close()no more messages go in

(2) send fails with err.full when the message is longer than the channel allows, and with err.cancelled once the channel is closed. receive fails with err.not_found on a channel that is closed and empty. Messages left in a closed channel are still taken.

(3) Only the task that called waits (14.2); the other tasks of the state go on. Only runs the host loop runs (pinax_loop_start) wait. In any other run, a send or receive that would have to wait ends the run with the fault PINAX_ERR_STATE.

(4) The host loop runs states on a set number of threads. pinax_loop_open takes a configuration: the number of threads, how many runs it holds at once, how much a host operation’s results may take, and one block of memory, as a state takes one: the loop’s objects are fixed slots in it (pinax_loop_size bytes), and each channel carves its slots from the same block when it is opened (pinax_channel_size bytes). Nothing is allocated while runs go on; with no block the loop takes one piece of that size from proven’s heap. A state runs on one thread at a time. A run whose budget (19.5) is used up goes to the back of the line, and a run that waits gives its thread up. While the host waits in pinax_loop_wait, when every run left waits for a channel and no host operation is outstanding, the loop ends all of them with PINAX_ERR_DEADLOCK.

17-channel.c

#include "pinax.h"
#include "pinax_loop.h"
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* One state sends the numbers 1 to 100 through the channel `jobs`; two others take them and
   add them up. The loop runs the three on two threads. */
static const char producer[] =
    "use jobs .\nuse str .\n"
    "def produce n int gives r int do\n"
    "  1 to i\n"
    "  loop\n"
    "    i n gt if break . end\n"
    "    i str.to_str jobs.send or_else to e -1 return end\n"
    "    i 1 add to i\n"
    "  end\n"
    "  jobs.close\n"
    "  n\n"
    "end\n";
static const char consumer[] =
    "use jobs .\nuse str .\n"
    "def consume n int gives r int do\n"
    "  0 to total\n"
    "  loop\n"
    "    jobs.receive or_else to e \"\" end to m      rem not_found: closed and empty\n"
    "    m str.is_empty if break . end\n"
    "    m str.to_int or_else to e 0 end total add to total\n"
    "  end\n"
    "  total\n"
    "end\n";

typedef struct worker {
    unsigned char block[1 << 20];
    pinax_state *state;
    pinax_word word;
    int64_t in, out;
    pinax_args args;
    pinax_err outcome;
} worker;
static worker w[3];

static void done(void *user, pinax_state *state, pinax_err outcome) {
    (void)state;
    ((worker *)user)->outcome = outcome;
}

static int start(pinax_loop *loop, pinax_channel *jobs, worker *x, const char *source, const char *word) {
    pinax_config config = {.struct_size = sizeof config, .budget = 1000};
    if (pinax_open((pinax_mem){x->block, sizeof x->block}, &config, &x->state) != PINAX_OK ||
        pinax_channel_register(x->state, jobs) != PINAX_OK ||
        pinax_load(x->state, "main", (pinax_str){(const unsigned char *)source, strlen(source)}, PINAX_LOAD_CODE) ||
        pinax_find(x->state, word, "(n int gives r int)", 0, &x->word) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    x->args = (pinax_args){.i = &x->in, .ri = &x->out};
    return pinax_loop_start(loop, x->state, x->word, &x->args, done, x) != PINAX_OK;
}

int main(void) {
    // the loop and its channel live in one block the host sizes with the two size functions
    pinax_loop_config loop_config = {.struct_size = sizeof loop_config, .threads = 2, .states = 3};
    static unsigned char loop_block[1 << 16];
    if (pinax_loop_size(&loop_config) + pinax_channel_size(&loop_config, 4, 20) > sizeof loop_block)
        return 1;
    loop_config.block = (pinax_mem){loop_block, sizeof loop_block};
    pinax_loop *loop;
    pinax_channel *jobs;
    if (pinax_loop_open(&loop_config, &loop) != PINAX_OK || pinax_channel_open(loop, "jobs", 4, 20, &jobs) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    w[0].in = 100;
    if (start(loop, jobs, &w[1], consumer, "consume") || start(loop, jobs, &w[2], consumer, "consume") ||
        start(loop, jobs, &w[0], producer, "produce"))
        return 1;
    pinax_loop_wait(loop);
    printf("sent %lld, received %lld\n", (long long)w[0].out, (long long)(w[1].out + w[2].out));

    /* the channel is closed and empty now: one more receiver ends at once */
    w[1].in = 0;
    if (pinax_loop_start(loop, w[1].state, w[1].word, &w[1].args, done, &w[1]) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    pinax_loop_wait(loop);
    printf("after close: %lld\n", (long long)w[1].out);

    /* a receiver on a channel nobody sends to: every run left waits, so the loop ends it */
    pinax_channel *idle;
    pinax_close(w[2].state);
    if (pinax_channel_open(loop, "jobs", 1, 20, &idle) != PINAX_OK || start(loop, idle, &w[2], consumer, "consume"))
        return 1;
    pinax_loop_wait(loop);
    printf("nobody sends: %s\n", w[2].outcome == PINAX_ERR_DEADLOCK ? "deadlock" : "?");
    pinax_loop_close(loop);
    for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k)
        pinax_close(w[k].state);
    return 0;
}

Output

$ ./17-channel
sent 100, received 5050
after close: 0
nobody sends: deadlock

17.5 sh — commands§

(1) sh runs commands through the system shell (/bin/sh -c; cmd.exe /c on Windows). pnx registers it; a host that embeds the library registers it only for scripts that may run commands (pinax_host_register(state,
"sh"); pinax_host_register_all does not), and the WebAssembly host has no sh.

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
sh.run(cmd str gives status int or fail)runs cmd; its output goes where the program’s goes, after what the program wrote. The status is the command’s: a status other than 0 is not a failure. Fails only when no shell can be started
sh.output(cmd str gives out str or fail)runs cmd and gives what it wrote on standard output, as written (with its line breaks), in the region
sh.output_into(cmd str, buf buffer gives status int or fail)the same, appended to a buffer; err.full when it does not fit (the command is read to its end)
sh.open_read(cmd str gives owned file or fail)a pipe from the command’s standard output, as a file (17.2): file.read_line, file.read, file.close
sh.open_write(cmd str gives owned file or fail)a pipe to the command’s standard input: file.write, file.close
sh.status(gives int)the status of the last command that ended: by run, output, output_into, or a pipe’s file.close, which waits for its command
sh.quote(s str gives str)s as one word for the system shell, to build a command from data: in single quotes for /bin/sh; in double quotes for cmd.exe, where % and ! keep their meaning
sh.cd(path str or fail)changes the working directory of the process; err.not_found when it cannot
sh.cwd(gives path str or fail)the working directory
sh.setenv(name str, value str or fail)sets an environment variable for the commands that follow (and env.getenv)
sh.exit(status int)ends the program with that status (0 to 255; others are clamped), after what is held back is written. The run stops there; in pnx repl the session ends

17-sh.pnx

use io .
use sh .
def main or fail do
  "echo one; echo two" sh.output or_fail io.print
  args "status " "exit 4" sh.run or_fail . cat io.println
  args "echo " "it's here" sh.quote . cat sh.output or_fail io.print
end
main or_else to e args "failed: " e err_text . cat io.println end

Output

$ pnx 17-sh.pnx
one
two
status 4
it's here

(2) A status is the command’s exit code; a command ended by a signal has 128 plus the signal’s number. A command that cannot be found is a status (127 for /bin/sh), not a failure. A command with a zero byte in it is err.argument. A write to a pipe whose command has stopped reading fails (err.failed). sh.status and sh.exit are of the thread that runs the state.

17.6 sqlite — databases§

(1) sqlite opens SQLite databases (files, or ":memory:") and runs SQL. pnx registers it; a host that embeds the library registers it with pinax_host_register_sqlite(state), a function of its own: pinax_host_register_all does not, pinax_host_register has no name for it, and a host that never calls it does not link SQLite. The WebAssembly host has no sqlite, and a pnx built without it (PNX_SQLITE=0) refuses use sqlite. A script that may use it may read and write any database file the process can open (also by ATTACH): register it as file is registered. A connection is the handle sqlite and a statement the handle stmt; both are owned when made and closed once (sqlite.close, sqlite.finalize).

ProcedureSignatureMeaning
sqlite.open(path str gives owned sqlite or fail)opens the database, creating it when it is not there; ":memory:" is a database in memory and "" a private temporary one. A path is a path: no file: names
sqlite.open_read(path str gives owned sqlite or fail)opens it read only; err.not_found when it cannot be opened
sqlite.close(db owned sqlite)closes the connection. A transaction left open is rolled back. Statements made on it keep working until they are finalized; the database closes with the last one
sqlite.exec(sql str, db sqlite or fail)runs the statements of sql, one after the other, and drops any rows. For text the program wrote; values go through bind_*
sqlite.scalar_int(sql str, db sqlite gives n int or fail)the first column of the first row, which must be an integer (err.format); err.not_found when there is no row
sqlite.scalar_str(sql str, db sqlite gives s str or fail)the same as a text (an integer or a real is given in its text form; a null or a blob is err.format)
sqlite.changes(db sqlite gives n int)the rows the last statement that wrote changed
sqlite.last_id(db sqlite gives n int)the row number the last insert made
sqlite.in_transaction(db sqlite gives bool)whether a transaction is open
sqlite.busy_ms(ms int, db sqlite or fail)how long a locked database is waited for; 0 (the start) does not wait
sqlite.prepare(sql str, db sqlite gives owned stmt or fail)one statement. Text after it that is more than space and comments, and a text with no statement, is err.format
sqlite.finalize(s owned stmt)
sqlite.reset(s stmt or fail)runs the statement from the start again; the values bound stay
sqlite.clear_binds(s stmt)binds null to every place
sqlite.bind_null(i int, s stmt or fail)binds place i, counted from 0. A place that is not there is err.range; a statement that is running (not reset since its last row or its end) is err.state
sqlite.bind_int sqlite.bind_str sqlite.bind_blob(v int, i int, s stmt or fail) and (v str, i int, s stmt or fail)bind an integer, a text or bytes (copied)
sqlite.bind_float(v float, i int, s stmt or fail)binds a real. A NaN or an infinity is err.range (SQLite turns a NaN into null)
sqlite.bind_name(name str, s stmt gives i int or fail)the place of :name, @name or $name (written with its mark); err.not_found when there is none
sqlite.rows(s stmt gives rail)a rail: each turn takes a step and gives the number of the row, from 0; it ends when there is no row (10.6 (1e))
sqlite.step(s stmt gives more bool or fail)takes one step: true when a row is there, false at the end
sqlite.col_count(s stmt gives n int)the columns of the result
sqlite.col_name(i int, s stmt gives name str or fail)the name of column i (from 0); err.range outside
sqlite.col_kind(i int, s stmt gives k int)the kind of the value in column i of the current row: sqlite.k_null, k_int, k_real, k_text or k_blob (pure procedures). With no row it is k_null. A column that is not there is the fault range
sqlite.col_is_null(i int, s stmt gives bool)whether it is null
sqlite.col_int(i int, s stmt gives n int or fail)an integer column; any other kind is err.format, no row err.not_found
sqlite.col_float(i int, s stmt gives x float or fail)a real column, or an integer column as the nearest float; any other kind is err.format, no row err.not_found
sqlite.col_str sqlite.col_blob(i int, s stmt gives v str or fail)a text, or bytes, in the region. col_str also gives an integer or a real in its text form; col_blob takes only a blob
sqlite.col_str_into sqlite.col_blob_into(i int, s stmt, buf buffer or fail)the same appended to a buffer; err.full when it does not fit
sqlite.last_code(gives n int)the SQLite result code (extended, for example 2067 for a unique key) of the last refusal of the thread that runs the state
sqlite.last_error(gives msg str)SQLite’s text for it (at most 255 bytes)

17-sqlite.pnx

use io .
use sqlite .
def main or fail do
  ":memory:" sqlite.open or_fail to db
  defer db sqlite.close end
  "create table fruit (name text primary key, price int)" db sqlite.exec or_fail
  "insert into fruit values (?, ?)" db sqlite.prepare or_fail to ins
  defer ins sqlite.finalize end
  "apple" 0 ins sqlite.bind_str or_fail
  3 1 ins sqlite.bind_int or_fail
  ins sqlite.step or_fail drop
  ins sqlite.reset or_fail
  "pear" 0 ins sqlite.bind_str or_fail
  5 1 ins sqlite.bind_int or_fail
  ins sqlite.step or_fail drop
  "select name, price from fruit order by price desc" db sqlite.prepare or_fail to q
  defer q sqlite.finalize end
  loop
    q sqlite.step or_fail
    not if break . end
    args 0 q sqlite.col_str or_fail " " 1 q sqlite.col_int or_fail . cat io.println
  end
  args "rows " "select count(*) from fruit" db sqlite.scalar_int or_fail . cat io.println
end
main or_else to e args "failed: " e err_text " " sqlite.last_error . cat io.println end

Output

$ pnx 17-sqlite.pnx
pear 5
apple 3
rows 2

17-sqlite-rows.pnx

use sqlite .
use io .
use str .
def listing db sqlite or fail do
  "create table t (id integer primary key, name text)" db sqlite.exec or_fail
  "insert into t (name) values ('a'), ('b'), ('c'), ('d')" db sqlite.exec or_fail
  "select id, name from t order by id" db sqlite.prepare or_fail to q
  defer q sqlite.finalize end
  q sqlite.rows do to n                                  rem the number of the row; the columns are read on the statement
    args n " " 0 q sqlite.col_int or_fail " " 1 q sqlite.col_str or_fail . cat io.println
  end each or_fail
  q sqlite.reset or_fail
  q sqlite.rows head 2 do to n n str.to_str io.println end each or_fail     rem lazy: no third step
end
def main or fail do
  ":memory:" sqlite.open or_fail to db
  defer db sqlite.close end
  db listing or_fail
end
main or_else to e "failed" io.println end

17-sqlite-float.pnx

use sqlite .
use io .
use f .
def demo or fail do
  ":memory:" sqlite.open or_fail to db
  defer db sqlite.close end
  "create table t (k integer, x real, s text)" db sqlite.exec or_fail
  "insert into t values (?, ?, ?)" db sqlite.prepare or_fail to ins
  defer ins sqlite.finalize end
  1 0 ins sqlite.bind_int or_fail  0.1e0 1 ins sqlite.bind_float or_fail  "a" 2 ins sqlite.bind_str or_fail
  ins sqlite.step or_fail drop  ins sqlite.reset or_fail

  1e0 0e0 f.div 1 ins sqlite.bind_float or_else to e args "inf: " e err_text . cat io.println end

$ pnx 17-sqlite-float.pnx
nan: range

1.0 0.1 true
2.0 -2.5e300 true

(2) A refusal of SQLite is a failure with one of these codes: err.full (out of memory, the disk full, a value too large), err.not_found (a file that cannot be opened, no row), err.range (a place that is not there), err.format (a file that is not a database, a statement that does not parse, a column of another kind), err.state (a statement used while it runs), and err.failed for the rest (a busy or locked database, a constraint, a read only database, an input or output error); sqlite.last_code tells which. In this edition sqlite has no procedures for a real column: a real column is read as a text (sqlite.col_str) and moved with str.to_float (7.7) or str.to_dec (7.5), and money is bound as an integer in its smallest unit.

(3) The memory SQLite uses is limited for the process: past a hard limit (256 MiB unless the host sets another) an allocation fails as err.full. A connection is used by one thread at a time, as the state it belongs to is. A call that waits for the disk holds the thread; no procedure is awaitable. A connection opens with defensive settings: no extensions are loaded, a database cannot be damaged by PRAGMA, and a statement is at most 16 MiB of text.

18 Calling C functions§

Syntax
extern = [ "export" ] "extern" c-name effect "from" STRING [ "as" NAME ] "end" ;
c-name = NAME | reserved-procedure | STRING ;

(1) extern NAME signature from "LIBRARY" end makes one C function a procedure. The processor does not open libraries itself. At load it asks the host’s resolver for (library, name) and calls the function the host gives. When the host has set no resolver, or gives no function, the load is refused. So the C functions a script can call are the host’s choice.

(2) With as OTHER at the end the script calls it by that name; the name asked of the host stays the same. When the name of the C function is a core procedure or a reserved word, or holds characters that are not those of a name (it is then written in quotes), as is required.

(3) The signature may have: as arguments int (and bool, narrow integers (7.6), declared types and other values represented as int), handles, str and cstr; as the result one int or handle, or none. or fail goes only with a handle result: a null pointer from the function is a failure. cstr is a type of this signature only.

(3a) A declared type (7.4) is passed as the type it is declared over: after type label str a label is a str to the C function, and a result of a type over u8 is checked as a u8 result is. Calls in the script still take the declared type, not its base.

(4) How the function is called: every int and every handle’s object pointer is one intptr_t argument; a str is two arguments, (const char *, size_t), not NUL-terminated; a cstr is one const char * to a NUL-terminated copy. At most eight C arguments. The result is read as one intptr_t. Functions of other shapes (floating point arguments, an int result, structs, variable arguments) are wrapped in host procedures.

18-extern.c

#include "pinax.h"
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Two C functions the script names. Every integer is an intptr_t; a str is (pointer, length). */
static intptr_t gcd(intptr_t a, intptr_t b) {
    while (b) { intptr_t t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}
static intptr_t count_vowels(const char *s, size_t n) {
    intptr_t k = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        k += strchr("aeiou", s[i]) != NULL && s[i] != '\0';
    return k;
}

/* The host decides what "mathlib" means: here, a table of its own functions. */
static pinax_extern_fn resolve(void *user, pinax_str library, pinax_str symbol) {
    (void)user;
    if (library.len != 7 || memcmp(library.ptr, "mathlib", 7) != 0)
        return NULL;
    if (symbol.len == 3 && memcmp(symbol.ptr, "gcd", 3) == 0)
        return (pinax_extern_fn)gcd;
    if (symbol.len == 12 && memcmp(symbol.ptr, "count_vowels", 12) == 0)
        return (pinax_extern_fn)count_vowels;
    return NULL;
}

static void try_load(pinax_state *st, const char *name, const char *text) {
    if (pinax_load(st, name, (pinax_str){(const unsigned char *)text, strlen(text)}, PINAX_LOAD_CODE) != PINAX_OK) {
        pinax_str why = pinax_error_text(st);
        printf("%s: %.*s\n", name, (int)why.len, (const char *)why.ptr);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    static unsigned char block[1 << 20];
    pinax_config config = {.struct_size = sizeof config};
    pinax_state *st;
    if (pinax_open((pinax_mem){block, sizeof block}, &config, &st) != PINAX_OK)
        return 1;
    pinax_set_resolver(st, resolve, NULL);
    try_load(st, "main",
             "extern gcd a int, b int gives int from \"mathlib\" end\n"
             "extern count_vowels s str gives int from \"mathlib\" as vowels end\n"
             "def answer gives int do 84 36 gcd \"embeddable\" vowels add end\n");
    pinax_word w;
    int64_t out = 0;
    pinax_find(st, "answer", "(gives int)", 0, &w);
    pinax_run(st, w, &(pinax_args){.ri = &out});
    printf("gcd(84, 36) + vowels(\"embeddable\") = %lld\n", (long long)out);

    try_load(st, "other", "extern sqrt x int gives int from \"libm\" end\n");   /* the host gives no such thing */
    pinax_close(st);
    return 0;
}

Output

$ ./18-extern
gcd(84, 36) + vowels("embeddable") = 16
other: extern: the host does not give this function

(5) A signature that does not match the C function is undefined behaviour in C, and the processor cannot know. A host that runs scripts it does not trust sets no resolver, or a typed one (6).

(5a) A typed resolver (pinax_set_typed_resolver) answers with the function and its C layout: the kind of each argument (an integer, a str as pointer and length, a cstr, a handle of a named type, owned or not), the kind of the result and whether the declaration says or fail. The load compares it with the layout the declaration makes and refuses a difference (PINAX_ERR_SIGNATURE; the message gives both). The script’s parameter names and its types over int do not matter, only what is passed. Once a typed resolver is set on a state, pinax_set_resolver is refused on it and its clones; on a state opened from an image it checks every C function of the image at once. A layout that matches does not make the function safe: the script still chooses every value.

Constraints

(6) A function whose name exists already (a core procedure, for instance) shall be given another name with as.

18-extern-as.pnx

extern abs n int gives int from "libc" end

Refused

$ pnx 18-extern-as.pnx
18-extern-as.pnx:1:8: this name is already defined: give the function another with `as`

(7) A signature that (3) does not allow is refused.

18-extern-result.pnx
